What 750,000 users taught me about building for the first 10.

A few years ago, I wanted to get closer to the startup ecosystem. Through Ministry of Programming in Sarajevo, I got closer to founders, product decisions, and how startup teams think. Later, I wanted to broaden that perspective, so I moved to Stockholm.

I spent 3.5 years there, surrounded by founders, product people, and startup teams. During that time, I worked on Bower, a product that reached around 750,000 users.

That experience changed how I think about products. I was not just writing code. I had the chance to take ownership of features, define problems, plan solutions, listen to feedback, and feel accountable for the experience real people were having.

When hundreds of thousands of people use something you helped build, small things stop being small. A confusing step becomes friction, a slow flow becomes frustration, and an unclear message becomes support work.

That matters even more today, when building and shipping has never been easier. You can add another button, label, flow, or screen quickly.

But the harder question is:

Should you?

Does it reduce the burden for the user, or does it only make the product feel more complete from the builder’s side?

One thing that stayed with me from Bower was the 30 second rule. From opening the product to feeling value, the user should not have to fight the interface, search around, or overthink what to do next.

After those years in Stockholm, I came back to Sarajevo.

Being part of the Techstars Founder Catalyst program helped me connect that product mindset with this market. Mentors from Bosnia and Herzegovina and around the world helped me see gaps I was missing, especially around sales, positioning, and how experts make decisions.

Now, while building Comit, I use that same mindset. Even though we are early, I try to build as if the platform already had hundreds of thousands of users. Not because of the number, but because of the responsibility.

Recently, one expert invited his first client to follow a plan through Comit. After seeing how much easier it was for him, and how much clearer it was for the client, he invited two more clients right away.

That felt good, but it did not feel random.

It came from simplifying the experience again and again.

Comit has two experiences that need to work together: the expert experience and the client experience. The expert side has to feel professional, flexible, and useful. The client side has to feel simple, clear, and easy to follow.

If one side feels heavy, the whole product suffers.

That is the part I care about most.

Comit is not just a place for plans, videos, exercises, or feedback.

It helps experts deliver their work with more structure, less chaos, and a better experience for the people they help.

Working on a product with scale taught me something I bring into Comit every day:

You do not earn trust with features.

You earn it by making the next step feel obvious.
hook: What 750,000 users taught me about building for the first 10.

Not because they're lazy. Because they have no system.

Here's how to build one in an afternoon:

The only topics you'll ever post about. No more staring at a blank page wondering what to write.

Step 2: Set your posting days
Three times a week is enough to get started. Block it in your calendar like a client meeting. Non-negotiable.

Step 3: Capture ideas as they happen
Keep a note on your phone. Good client question? Write it down. Solved a problem? Write it down. Your content bank fills itself.

Step 4: Batch write once a week
90 minutes. All your posts for the week, done in one sitting. No context switching. No daily guilt.

We built Postiv exactly for this step. Every Monday, Bob drafts your full week of posts based on your pillars and source material. You review, tweak, approve. Done.

Step 5: Schedule and close the tab
15 minutes to review and schedule. Then you're done until next week.

That's the whole system.

Most people overcomplicate LinkedIn. The ones who win just show up with a process behind them.

"What's your team vision?"
Most leaders answer with a number. Revenue. OKRs. Q4 targets.
That's the boring half.

A team vision isn't just what you want to achieve. It's who you want to be while achieving it.

For my own team, that means:
— Small. Max seven people. 
— Kind. Fun. The kind of energy you can feel on a call. 
— Conflict-friendly. No tiptoeing. 
— Feedback as a default, not an event. 
— AI and tools wherever they buy us back time for what matters.

All of it shapes how the work actually gets done.

Try this: set a timer for 10 minutes and answer three questions.
What actually motivates me? 
What motivates my teammates? 
What's our team vision — beyond the numbers?

Then have your team do the same.

The gaps in your answers? That's the conversation worth having.

I’ve coached Ivy grads, PhDs, refugees, non-target students, and college dropouts into McKinsey, BCG, and Bain.

Different backgrounds.

Same private fear.

“Maybe I’m just not good enough.”

Not smart enough.

Not polished enough.

Not strategic enough.

Not from the right school.

Not from the right country.

Not from the right life story.

And here is the part most candidates never see:

The strongest profiles often carry the loudest doubt.

The target-school MBA worries he is not differentiated enough.

The PhD worries she sounds too academic.

The non-target candidate assumes the game was already lost before it started.

The experienced professional wonders whether it is too late to pivot.

Different story.

Same question:

“Who do you think you are?”

But that question is a trap.

Because MBB does not hire people because they feel ready.

MBB hires people who can remove doubt.

Doubt about their thinking.

Doubt about their judgment.

Doubt about their communication.

Doubt about whether a partner would trust them in front of a client.

That is the real game.

Most candidates ask the wrong question:

“Am I good enough?”

That question keeps them stuck.

They delay.

They overthink.

They practice randomly.

They do cases with other people who also do not know the bar.

They watch more videos.

They collect more frameworks.

They call it preparation.

But often, it is just fear wearing a productivity costume.

The better question is:

“Am I preparing in a way that would make an MBB interviewer comfortable betting on me?”

That is a completely different standard.

Not confidence.

Not motivation.

Not potential.

Evidence.

Evidence that you can structure messy problems.

Evidence that you can think under pressure.

Evidence that you can communicate like someone who belongs in the room.

Evidence that your personal stories show real ownership, not polished storytelling.

That evidence does not appear because you wait long enough.

It is built.

Deliberately.

With the right structure.

The right feedback.

The right standard.

The right people around you.

You do not land an MBB offer because fear disappears.

You land it because your preparation becomes strong enough that fear no longer controls the outcome.

So if you are afraid, fine.

That does not disqualify you.

But guessing your way through preparation might.

If McKinsey, BCG, or Bain is your serious goal this year, prepare like the goal is real.

Thomas Power was 16, behind the deli counter at Waitrose, when he noticed something odd.

He could remember every customer's order.

Not roughly. Exactly.

The weight. The cut. Whether the family wanted their meat thick or thin.
He also noticed that richer families wanted it thick. Poorer families wanted it thin - because they needed to make it stretch for the children.

He had no idea why his brain was collecting all of this.

He just couldn't stop it.

Forty years later, Thomas has been trained by Alan Sugar, Michael Dell, and Steve Ballmer. He built a social business network four years before LinkedIn existed. He survived stage three bowel cancer. He is 62 and currently outpacing people a third of his age.

And his brain is still doing exactly what it did at that deli counter.

In this clip, he describes it like this:

"My mind is very focused on patterns, shapes, trends and memes... depending on your neurodivergent profile, you'll handle the data in a different way."

No diagnosis. No label. No performance.

Just a man describing, plainly, what his brain has been doing his entire life.

And, quietly, what it built.

Some of you have been doing this since you were children.

Collecting data no one asked you to collect.

Seeing the shape of something three conversations before it had a name.

Being told you overthink. That you're too intense. That you're "a lot."

Yeah. You were seeing around corners in a world that hadn't built any yet.

The question was never whether your brain was capable.

It was whether you'd stop apologising for it long enough to find out what it could actually do.

Drop a 🧩 if your brain is currently running pattern analysis on something no one else has clocked yet.

Or come find me in the DMs - I'd love to hear what you're seeing.

body:
After spending years thinking through difficult situations, making mistakes in past projects, and building my mindset through those experiences, I wanted to share a few tricks that helped me make successful decisions more clearly and confidently even when I don’t have full visibility.

Effective decision making is one of the key features of a successful project manager. Sometimes there are a lot of uncertainties around you, but you are still expected to decide like there is none.

A game-changing moment for me was when I read The Paradox of Choice by Barry Schwartz.

The paradox of choice suggests that having more options often leads to worse decisions and less satisfaction instead of better outcomes.

Here are a few practical ways to apply it:

➡️ Limit your options
Before researching, cap your choices at 3–5. More than that usually creates analysis paralysis.

➡️ Decide what’s “good enough”
Try to be a “satisficer” instead of a “maximizer.” Define your minimum requirements upfront and stop once they’re met instead of endlessly searching for the perfect option.

➡️ Make reversible decisions fast
If a decision can easily be undone, don’t overthink it. Save your mental energy for decisions with long-term consequences.

➡️ Set a time limit
Give yourself a deadline even for small decisions. Constraints force clarity.

➡️ Stop comparing after choosing
Post-decision comparison usually creates regret, not improvement. Once you decide, move forward confidently.

➡️ Categorize decisions by impact
High-impact decisions deserve deep thinking. Low-impact decisions deserve speed. Most people do the opposite.

➡️ Build routines and defaults
Automating repetitive decisions reduces mental fatigue and frees your focus for more important challenges.

The biggest insight for me was this:
Freedom of choice improves life only up to a certain point. After that point, it can actually work against clarity and confidence.

Developer is my middle name with tools like Claude Code😅

Yesterday I built an app in 2 hours that lets SEO agencies capture leads by giving prospects a simple tool to analyze their presence in AI search and turn them into clients (Thanks
Katerina Fotiadi
for the idea 🙌)

Spoiler: the excitement around this is justified. Just check the recording below to see how it works👇 

And the first thing I did was stop overthinking it.
I just told Claude what I needed, even though my needs were pretty vague.

After setting up Claude Code (I used it in the terminal, btw) and connecting the SE Ranking API via MCP (to pull real data), I gave it a pretty simple prompt:

"Build a lead magnet web app where a user enters their domain and sees how their brand stacks up against top competitors in AI search engines (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, AI Overview, AI Mode). Output a leaderboard with a CTA to hire the agency."

The user flow ended up being:
1️⃣ User lands on homepage
2️⃣ Enters domain + selects country + AI engines
3️⃣ Clicks “Analyze my AI visibility”
4️⃣ Gets a loading screen (~15–20 sec)
5️⃣ Sees results:
- AI Rank, Share of Voice, brand mentions, link citations
- Engine breakdown (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, etc.)
- Leaderboard vs competitors
- CTA to convert

Of course, it didn't work perfectly on the first try.
To be honest, I didn't fully understand what I was building at that point. So I just kept asking Claude to fix things, explain what it was doing, and why.

And after about 5–6 rounds of fixes, it worked.

My takeaways:
💡 The doors vibe coding opens are real. All you really need is a great idea. The rest can actually come together much faster than you think.
🤔 For me, this was just a random Tuesday afternoon test. But for an agency or business, this is already something more: a lead magnet, a client audit tool, or even a standalone product. All built before dinner. Just saying… 👀
⚠️ That said, if you're building something serious, you'll still may run into edge cases, and that’s where you’ll want an expert to sanity-check things. Don’t underestimate that part.

Huge thanks to the
SE Ranking
team,
Guifré Ballester
, and
Anastasia Kotsiubynska
for the workshop that inspired me to kick this off 🙌

A CTA from me: if you've been sitting on an idea (personal or work-related) - this is your sign to just try it✨

And let me know if you have any questions in the comments below! 👇

Ideas are cheap. Execution is everything.

Most people are waiting. They are waiting for the "perfect" idea, the "perfect" market conditions, or—the biggest trap of all—the approval of the people around them.

Here is the truth: The moment you stop waiting and actually start, everything changes.

When you begin to relentlessly chase your dreams and build your business, you don’t just build a product; you transform your entire reality. You build discipline, resilience, and a dynamic mindset.

But what about the fear of judgment?

The fastest way to kill your potential is to care about "what other people might think." The opinion of onlookers won’t build your future, and it certainly won’t pay your bills. If you are not doing something that makes comfortable people uncomfortable with your ambition, you are playing it too safe.

Stop planning for "one day." Start creating today.

You can't steer a parked car. Get it moving first, then adjust the direction.

What is the one project you are delaying right now because of overthinking? Stop waiting. Start executing.

body:
There are two types of people in every organization, and the room above you has already decided which one you are.

Complexifiers and simplifiers.

A complexifier makes things harder than they need to be. 
• They ask too many questions, most of them unnecessary.
• They overthink the brief before they have done the first 20 minutes of work on it. 
• They want one more meeting before they decide. 
• They send you a message that says, "I've put the information in the document" without the link, so now you have to find the document, open it, scan 30 pages, and figure out which part was the answer to your question.

A simplifier figures it out. 
• They are resourceful. 
• They get the thing done with the information already in the room. When they finish, they send you a message that says, "I've completed it. Here's a three-line summary of what's inside. Link to the full document at the bottom if you want to go deeper." You decide in 90 seconds instead of 90 minutes. 
  
The behavioural contrast is not subtle once you start watching for it.

🚫 A complexifier escalates a decision two levels up that they had the authority to make. 
✅ A simplifier makes the call, documents the reasoning, and tells you what they decided.

🚫 A complexifier sends an agenda with seven items and no decisions sought. 
✅ A simplifier sends three items and the decision required against each one.

🚫 A complexifier flags a problem. 
✅ A simplifier flags a problem and the two routes through it, with a recommendation.

🚫 A complexifier asks, "Do you have a minute?" without saying what for. 
✅ A simplifier writes the minute they need, before they ask for it.

The promotion conversation in the closed room is not about who is smarter, who works harder, or who has the better strategy. 

It is about who makes the room lighter. The people backed at senior levels are almost always simplifiers, because the room above them is already drowning in complexity.

I used to be a complexifier. I asked questions to demonstrate I was thinking. I sent long emails to demonstrate I had done the work. Every one of those moves was a tax on the people above me, and the tax was being noticed.

That is the careerquake nobody names. The disruption is the slow realisation that the people getting backed around you are not the ones with better answers. They are the ones who made it easier for the room above them to back them.

The good news is that being a simplifier is a learnable set of behaviours, not a personality. 

It is the difference between writing the email that takes you 12 minutes and saves the reader 4, and writing the email that takes you 4 minutes and costs the reader 12. 

The first one gets you promoted. 
The second one is invisible to you because you are the one writing it.

This is part of what we teach inside our 8-week program, From Hidden Talent to Visible Leader. The cohort starts next Monday.

Which one were you in the last email you sent?

Developer is my middle name with tools like Claude Code😅

Yesterday I built an app in 2 hours that lets SEO agencies capture leads by giving prospects a simple tool to analyze their presence in AI search and turn them into clients (Thanks
Katerina Fotiadi
for the idea 🙌)

Spoiler: the excitement around this is justified. Just check the recording below to see how it works👇 

And the first thing I did was stop overthinking it.
I just told Claude what I needed, even though my needs were pretty vague.

After setting up Claude Code (I used it in the terminal, btw) and connecting the SE Ranking API via MCP (to pull real data), I gave it a pretty simple prompt:

"Build a lead magnet web app where a user enters their domain and sees how their brand stacks up against top competitors in AI search engines (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, AI Overview, AI Mode). Output a leaderboard with a CTA to hire the agency."

The user flow ended up being:
1️⃣ User lands on homepage
2️⃣ Enters domain + selects country + AI engines
3️⃣ Clicks “Analyze my AI visibility”
4️⃣ Gets a loading screen (~15–20 sec)
5️⃣ Sees results:
- AI Rank, Share of Voice, brand mentions, link citations
- Engine breakdown (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, etc.)
- Leaderboard vs competitors
- CTA to convert

Of course, it didn't work perfectly on the first try.
To be honest, I didn't fully understand what I was building at that point. So I just kept asking Claude to fix things, explain what it was doing, and why.

And after about 5–6 rounds of fixes, it worked.

My takeaways:
💡 The doors vibe coding opens are real. All you really need is a great idea. The rest can actually come together much faster than you think.
🤔 For me, this was just a random Tuesday afternoon test. But for an agency or business, this is already something more: a lead magnet, a client audit tool, or even a standalone product. All built before dinner. Just saying… 👀
⚠️ That said, if you're building something serious, you'll still may run into edge cases, and that’s where you’ll want an expert to sanity-check things. Don’t underestimate that part.

Huge thanks to the
SE Ranking
team,
Guifré Ballester
, and
Anastasia Kotsiubynska
for the workshop that inspired me to kick this off 🙌

A CTA from me: if you've been sitting on an idea (personal or work-related) - this is your sign to just try it✨

And let me know if you have any questions in the comments below! 👇

I spent a weekend inside Anthropic's finance agents repo.

It quietly rewrote how I'm building every agent on my roadmap.

Anthropic shipped 10 production-grade finance agents this week. Pitchbook builder. KYC screener. Month-end closer. The agents will get the headlines.

The architecture underneath is the actual story.

Every single agent is composed of exactly three pieces:

↳ Skills. Markdown files describing the workflow and domain knowledge.
↳ Connectors. Governed access to data like FactSet, Moody's, internal warehouses.
↳ Subagents. Focused Claude calls for sub-tasks like comparables selection.

That's it. Markdown and YAML. Forkable. Reviewable. The same template runs as a plugin in Cowork, in Claude Code, or as a managed agent.

I've been hand-rolling production agents for 18 months. Prompts in one place. Tool definitions in another. Audit trails bolted on after the fact. Every team I talk to is doing some version of the same thing.

Anthropic just gave the industry a shared vocabulary.

Here's what changed for me this week.

I pulled my roadmap open and asked three questions of every agent on it:

↳ What's the skill. The actual markdown workflow.
↳ What's the governed data access. The connector.
↳ What sub-tasks deserve their own focused Claude call.

Three questions. Decisions I'd been overthinking for weeks collapsed in an afternoon.

If you're building anything agentic right now, clone the repo and read one agent end to end. Pitch-agent or gl-reconciler are the cleanest starts. The skill files are short. The structure clicks fast.

It's the clearest reference I've seen for how a serious agent is actually put together.

Should you use the ‘Open to Work’ banner?

Here’s the straight answer 👇

The private ‘Open to Work’ setting on LinkedIn?

Turn it on. 

Every...
Single...
Time.

No debate.

Why?

Because recruiters use filters when they are searching for talent on LinkedIn Recruiter.

And if you’re not marked as open, you quite literally disappear from parts of their search results.

Invisible talent is not getting hired. Simple as that.

Also, super important to remember: it’s not visible publicly.

So your boss scrolling your profile won’t see it. Neither will the recruiters working at your company.

So there will be no awkward Monday morning chats needed!!

Now, what about the green public banner?

This is where we are opening Pandora's Box!! 

Some say: “It looks desperate.”

body:
In grad school I took an entire class on annotation, aka professionally overthinking whether people can agree on anything.

At first, I didn’t understand why we spent so much time focusing on things like Cohen’s κ, Fleiss’ κ, and Krippendorff’s α. We even learned to calculate the pairwise agreements needed for these metrics and other insights by hand (or, well, by code). 

By the end of the semester, though, one thing had become clear: these metrics were 𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘢𝘯𝘵. Not just for school or quality, but for a deep and clear understanding of how your annotators are working and the kind of data quality you can expect from a given group. 

Throughout my career, I’ve continued to use these metrics to get real signals from my data and annotators to make sure projects stay on track. Even if my skip level managers didn’t quite understand the math, having real numbers was a huge win for me and the teams that I was on.

All of which is to say: 𝙄 𝙘𝙖𝙧𝙚 𝙖 𝙡𝙤𝙩 𝙖𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙖𝙜𝙧𝙚𝙚𝙢𝙚𝙣𝙩.

And with that said, this newest release is extra fun for me. 

We just shipped 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗲𝗿-𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘂𝗹𝗮𝗿 𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗟𝗮𝗯𝗲𝗹 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗼 𝗘𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲.

One thing that’s always bugged me, both academically and in production, is how often agreement gets reduced to a single number.

A single score doesn’t tell you:
 • where annotators disagree
 • why they disagree
 • what to actually fix

Which, honestly, is kind of the whole point in the real world. 

So, here’s what we focused on:
  • 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻-𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 (𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸-𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹)
𝘚𝘰 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘱𝘪𝘯𝘱𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘵 𝘦𝘹𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘭𝘺 𝘸𝘩𝘪𝘤𝘩 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘢 𝘵𝘢𝘴𝘬 𝘪𝘴 𝘤𝘢𝘶𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘥𝘪𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘨𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦, 𝘪𝘯𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘢𝘥 𝘰𝘧 𝘤𝘩𝘢𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘩𝘶𝘯𝘤𝘩𝘦𝘴.
 • 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗱𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗲𝘀 (𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘀𝘂𝘀 𝘃𝘀. 𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗿𝘄𝗶𝘀𝗲)
𝘉𝘦𝘤𝘢𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭-𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘭𝘥 𝘴𝘦𝘵𝘶𝘱𝘴 𝘥𝘰𝘯’𝘵 𝘭𝘰𝘰𝘬 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘤𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘯, 2-𝘢𝘯𝘯𝘰𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘰𝘳 𝘴𝘤𝘦𝘯𝘢𝘳𝘪𝘰𝘴 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘵𝘦𝘹𝘵𝘣𝘰𝘰𝘬𝘴.
 • 𝗙𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 + 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗱𝘀 (𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵, 𝗜𝗼𝗨, 𝗝𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗱, 𝗲𝘁𝗰.)
𝘈𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘢𝘥𝘢𝘱𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘥𝘢𝘵𝘢 𝘮𝘰𝘥𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺, 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘰𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘸𝘢𝘺 𝘢𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘥.
 • 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘀, 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝘁𝗵
𝘐𝘯𝘤𝘭𝘶𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨𝘴 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘓𝘓𝘔-𝘢𝘴-𝘫𝘶𝘥𝘨𝘦, 𝘮𝘰𝘥𝘦𝘭 𝘷𝘴. 𝘮𝘰𝘥𝘦𝘭, 𝘰𝘳 𝘢𝘯𝘯𝘰𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘰𝘳 𝘷𝘴. 𝘨𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘳𝘶𝘵𝘩.

If you take one thing away from this post, let it be this:
𝗔𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗮 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰. 𝗜𝘁’𝘀 𝗮 𝗱𝗲𝗯𝘂𝗴𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮, 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗺𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺.

And they say you never use anything you learned in school in the real world.

#AI
AI will not replace you.

But someone who uses it better will.

That is already happening.

Last year, I wrote this:
The Age of Co-Creation - How
Al Is Rewiring Our Minds, Creativity, and Communication

Today, the gap is visible.

Not between experts and beginners.
Between people who act - and people who wait.

Here is the uncomfortable truth:

Most people are not behind because of AI.
They are behind because they do not use it.

What changed?

* Work is no longer about doing
* It is about directing
* Output is no longer power
* Clarity is
* Knowledge is no longer scarce
* Execution is

The winners right now:

* Test daily
* Ship fast
* Think in systems
* Use AI as leverage

The rest:

* Scroll
* Overthink

 "This is my instinct. There are many others like this, but this one is mine. I am a strong, powerful leader and believe in my gut feel above all else".

body:
This week's Patch Notes was a cathartic one to write.

I know its old news (what 7 days now) but Destiny is ending. Bungie confirmed that Destiny 2 gets its final content update on June 9, with layoffs to follow and no Destiny 3 in production. For a lot of people that's a headline. For me it's a swan song.

I have been a Bungie lifer since the LAN party days. Halo in the dorms, thousands of hours in Combat Evolved and Halo 2, then I followed the studio to Destiny and never really left. I ran King's Fall every weekend, six to nine every Saturday and Sunday for years. I bonded with my future Twitch colleagues over this game in a job interview before the interview even started. 

Destiny wasn't just a game I played. It was a fixture of my actual life.

So I wanted to do more than react to the news. After getting into it with
Greg Posner
on
Player Driven
earlier this week, it was clear a lot of people are mourning Bungie without the full context of how it got here, so I traced the whole arc... the recalled copy of Myth II in 1998, Microsoft saving the studio and then losing it, the Activision divorce and the champagne that flew when Bungie bought Destiny back, and finally Sony's $3.6 billion bet that's now been written down by three-quarters of a billion dollars.

The throughline is this. Bungie was a company that could never be owned. It walked away from Microsoft and gave up Halo. It walked away from Activision and kept Destiny. The same ungovernable streak that made it great is the same thing that made it impossible to hold together once there was no owner left to escape. 

The rebellion finally had nowhere to go, so it turned inward. 

And the part that stings most, backed by our mindGAME data showing Destiny 2 down ~89% from its 2019 peak (at least in our tracking which starts in 2019), is that the obvious lifeline, a Destiny 3, was the one thing the studio kept choosing not to build.

Bungie outlasted every owner it ever had. This time it couldn't outlast itself.
It's not all melancholy, though. The issue also gets into:

☑️  My LEGO Batman review with my son, and what "an Arkham game for kids" tells us about where the Batman franchise is headed 
☑️ Summer Game Fest, where I'll be on the floor in LA all next week
And the game I'm most fired up about: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. 

Revealed yesterday, locked for October 22, and in my read a billion-dollar game and a real S-tier contender after a rough Black Ops 7 year. Beyond that I'm watching Marvel's Wolverine, the GTA VI gravity well bending the entire calendar around it, the Fable delay that just proved my 2027 call, and a WB Games rumor mill I'm deeply skeptical can market its way home.

If you're going to be at SGF next week, find me on the floor.  I'll also be at
GamesBeat
's event next Thursday.

What did Destiny mean to you? I'd genuinely like to hear it.
hook: This week's Patch Notes was a cathartic one to write.

More people than ever ask me when PowerPoint will die.

I don't think it will. But the way we make presentations is about to fundamentally shift.

A lot of the "modern" AI tools are running the presentation race the wrong way. They build workflows where AI makes the slides and forgets the humans. A slide you can't edit isn't a slide. It's a screenshot. You can make that in Paint. The same goes for charts.

And charts are what separate important decision decks from regular presentations.

AI tools still struggle here. They struggle with quality. With making charts editable. With updating a recurring report built by AI last quarter. And when they do get it right, it takes forever and burns tokens. At scale, that's a real problem.

In consulting, banking, and strategy, the chart is the deliverable. When the CFO sends one revised number at 11pm, you need to fix it on the slide. Not regenerate the whole thing. Not rebuild the chart from scratch. Not explain to the partner why everything looks different now.

We've spent ten years at Grunt building the best slide automation engine for humans.

Now we're launching Grunt AI.

This is the moment Grunt stops being a productivity booster for professionals and becomes the vital toolkit for humans and machines building charts and business visualizations.

Grunt AI is cross-platform by design. It works natively inside PowerPoint, building real, fully editable, brand-compliant charts directly on your slides. It works in the browser. It works inside third-party chat agents. And it works as an MCP server enterprises can plug into their own internal AI solutions.

The same toolkit that lets a human build a great chart in seconds is what lets an AI build one too. And you can switch back and forth whenever you want.

32% target margin, 18% actual margin, 14 points of hidden costs that nobody planned for.

These aren't extreme cases I’d say, but is what average margin leakage looks like across pharma tenders, and most finance teams don't catch it until the tender is already running.

I've been thinking a lot about why this keeps happening, even in companies with strong finance functions.

The answer is that tender economics shift after the bid gets approved, and the models most teams use weren't built to move with them, not that people are bad at building models.

A small volume increase triggers a different rebate tier. Logistics costs go up by €0.30 per unit. Revenue recognition timing shifts. None of these are surprises on their own, but the model can't show you what they look like combined. So nobody sees the real margin until it's already gone.

We wrote about this in our latest ebook because it's a pattern we see across the industry.

The teams that manage tender profitability well aren't doing anything radical.
They simulate scenarios before they commit, they keep finance and commercial working in the same model, and they don't stop tracking once the bid is submitted.

Sounds simple, but most companies aren't set up for it yet.

body:
Two words that reveal you don't understand positioning: "brand positioning."

Position is the concept you own in someone's head — proven through decisions, not claimed through words.

Brand is the set of associations, expectations, and reputation that accumulates over time through interactions with your business.

Position is the foundation. 
Brand is what forms around it.

Volvo's position is Safety. Their brand (Swedish engineering, family-oriented, boxy design, practical premium) clusters around that core concept. Every association reinforces the anchor.

You don't position a brand.

You establish a position. Then the brand forms around it through consistent decisions over time.

"Brand positioning" implies you can shape perception (brand) by crafting the right message (positioning).

That's backwards. 
And it fails for a specific reason.

Explicit claims trigger skepticism. The moment you say "We're innovative," you activate defence mechanisms, customers recognize the marketing tactic, resist being told what to think, and infer you're serving your interests, not theirs.

Implicit proof bypasses all of this. When every decision proves a concept without stating it, customers draw their own conclusions. Self-generated inferences are more persuasive than any claim you could make.

Roger Martin watched GM spend years trying to "reposition" Oldsmobile through campaigns that claimed, "This is not your father's Oldsmobile."

The brand died anyway.

His verdict: "You can't stand for something that you aren't."

The failure wasn't the advertising. It was attempting to claim through messaging what couldn't be proven through product and experience.

Here's what practitioners miss:

Position is a strategic choice, the identity of the business itself. It shapes product decisions, operational priorities, and cultural values. And finally, communication.

Brand is what sticks after the market watches those choices accumulate.

You can craft a positioning statement (which most of you reading this do). You cannot craft a brand. The market does that for you by watching your business decisions, not reading your deck.

The only way to know your actual position? Watch what customers do automatically, not what they say when asked.

Stop saying "brand positioning."

Say positioning. 
Then make decisions that prove it.

The brand will follow, or it won't.

The market decides. 

Your job is to give it no other conclusion to reach.

body:
From my experience, prop trading firms don't have a scaling problem. They have an attribution mess disguised as operations.
Three things almost nobody fixes early enough:

1. They scale traffic before fixing attribution.
A trader clicks. Fills a form. Buys a challenge later. Upgrades later. Gets funded later. Buys again months later.
Every handoff is a chance to lose the affiliate ID. By the time anyone notices, the tracking logic is too tangled to fix without breaking ops.
So teams patch it with spreadsheets, manual checks, finance reconciliation, and "can you verify this commission?" Slack threads.
That's not scale. That's debt.

2. They accept fragmented reporting as normal.
Clicks in one dashboard. Payments in another. Affiliate data somewhere else. CRM disconnected from all of it.
And somehow the team is supposed to calculate accurate payouts across the whole trader lifecycle.
Prop attribution is harder than SaaS or ecommerce. Longer conversion path. More complex lifecycle. More aggressive payout structures. You can't run that on disconnected systems.
One source of truth isn't a feature anymore. It's infrastructure.

3. They underestimate the cost of manual reconciliation.
The real cost isn't payroll. It's trust.
Affiliates stop trusting the numbers. Partners question payouts. Ops becomes the bottleneck. Finance slows down. Leadership thinks the answer is more hires.
It almost never is. The infrastructure was never built for the volume.

The firms scaling affiliate programs cleanly aren't operationally smarter. They just fixed attribution before the chaos set.

Most firms wait until the chaos is permanent. Don't. DM and let's fix it.

Are you struggling to scale paid ads efficiently in 2026?

Here's 4 things I find myself repeatedly telling clients ⤵️

1/ Fix your plumbing

Your "plumbing" is your paid media infrastructure. 

This comprises everything from:

• Naming conventions
• Conversion tracking
• Reporting & alerts
• Campaign set up
  
This doesn't have to be rocket science, it just needs to be consistent. 

Based on your program's goals, budgets, regions, and segments. 

Devise a paid infrastructure that will allow you to easily:

• Pace budgets
• Report on progress
• Optimize based on KPIs

2/ Keep it simple, and repeatable 

You can't scale complicated.

Even if you have complicated problems, there's usually a simple answer. 

Unfortunately the smarter you are the harder this step will be. 

Ask yourself is this nice in theory but not in practice? 

Outside of ROI, don't forget the return on effort. 

3/ Slow down to speed up

Everything is urgent in startup land, and it never seems to stop. 

When it comes to paid media take the time for:

• Planning new experiments
• Writing down any learnings 

It might seem slower at first but you'll end up moving faster.

Building on your learnings while others repeat the same mistakes.

4/ Think big fish, small pond

I know you want to be the world's greatest {___} solution. 

But the reality is you're not spending $1M+/month in paid media.

Instead, focus your paid media dollars on your most profitable audience. 

For example:

• Instead of targeting all accounts, can we focus on Tier As? 
• Instead of showing ads 7/days week can we show them 5/days a week?
• Instead of targeting 5 personas, can we focus on our top 2?

You are probably leaving millions on the table because of your DSO formula. 

Top-performing companies have a DSO 18 days shorter than the median (Hackett, 2025). On a $100M revenue business, that's $5M of cash they don't have to borrow to fund their investments. At $1B, that's $50M of free bandwidth.

Meanwhile, most finance teams spend hundreds of thousands on cost reduction programs, close-cycle tools and reporting projects to get very limited savings. 

To join the top companies, you first have to measure DSO properly.

What you learned is:
DSO = (Accounts Receivable / Monthly Credit Sales) × 30.
The formula is correct... but misleading.

Think about it. Revenue from a big order in the last week of the month inflates the denominator. Standard DSO drops 7 days. But nobody paid faster. The metric just moved. Waves come but you measure wind.

This is why true measurement comes before action. 
The better measurement is: Countback DSO. 
Walk backward through credit sales until AR is exhausted. 
*That number* is your real DSO.

Run both this month. 
If they differ by more than 5 days, simple DSO is masking reality.

This week's Practical Lean Finance article walks through the worked example and the dollar gap to terms.

Next article will cover the actual DSO levers.

You think your conversations with Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, or Perplexity are private. They're not.

IMDEA Networks (Madrid) just published the receipts. While you asked ChatGPT about your symptoms, ran ideas past Claude, or shared your business plan with Grok, your data flowed to Meta, Google, TikTok, LinkedIn, and at least nine other ad platforms. Not by accident. By design.

The specifics are uglier than the headlines:
Claude routes user events server-side to eleven ad platforms from Anthropic's own infrastructure. Your browser ad-blocker can't see it. They proxy analytics through a first-party domain (
a-cdn.anthropic.com
) engineered to bypass hostname blockers. Email and conversation URLs go to Intercom every authenticated session, regardless of cookie consent.

ChatGPT sends conversation URLs and chat topics to Google Analytics for every free logged-in user, regardless of cookie choice.

Grok sends verbatim message content to TikTok(straight to the CCP)  via Open Graph metadata. Guest chats public by default.

Perplexity sent the same to Meta Pixel until Doe v. Perplexity, Meta, Google (N.D. Cal., March 2026). Removed in April.

Privacy policies don't lie outright. They use language like "business partners" and "content you submit" — broad enough to legally cover sending your medical conversation to Meta, narrow enough you'd never guess.

The bigger lie: that your data is anonymized.

For anyone doing novel research, sovereign work, regulated tech, journalism, or anything genuinely original, anonymization is mathematically impossible. The novelty is the identifier. Strip every name from your proprietary architecture and the architecture still names itself by being itself. Sweeney proved this in 2002. Narayanan and Shmatikov de-anonymized the Netflix Prize in 2008. The FTC admitted in 2024: hashing doesn't make data anonymous.
Here's where it stops being a privacy story.

When novel proprietary work from foreign nationals flows through US infrastructure subject to the CLOUD Act and FISA 702, processed by companies the government can compel under sealed legal process — under the Tallinn Manual 2.0, this is state-enabled espionage wearing commercial clothes.

The architecture isn't accident. The disclosures aren't negligence. "We don't train on your data" is calibrated to be technically true while you believe something broader. Privacy controls make you feel protected while extraction continues server-side, invisible, beyond your reach.

If you produce anything novel — research, code, strategy, journalism, legal work, government work — assume every conversation has been read by parties whose interests don't align with yours. Not paranoia. Calibration.

OpenAI

,
Gisli Olafsson
let's start a dialog for meaningful change before it's legislated.

Good luck. Have fun. Don't die.

Stanford tested 51 enterprise AI deployments.
77% of the hardest problems weren’t technical.
They were governance.

Read that as "we need more committees" and you’ve just rebuilt the old operating model under a new banner. Shadow AI doesn’t emerge because your formal channels lack principles — it emerges because they’re too slow to use. Another approval gate accelerates the exodus. It doesn’t stop it.

The correct reading is the opposite move.
Governance isn’t the brake. It’s the frame. Clear intent. Defined authorisations. Known guardrails. An auditable trail. Inside the frame, teams act fast because the scaffolding is already there. Outside the frame, every decision needs a committee — and every committee is a drag on the log-linear curve your technology is running on.

Standards are the instrument that delivers the frame at enterprise scale. That’s why Auditdata — at under 200 people — just became one of the first 50 companies in the world to certify ISO 42001, alongside our existing ISO 13485, MDR and ISO 27001.

25%

It's the most-cited, least-fulfilled number in European trucking law.

Directive 96/53/EC says at least 25% of a heavy truck's gross weight must rest on the drive axle. Sounds reasonable. Until you actually do the math.

A standard 40-ton EU semi-trailer on my last Sweden tour: 25.2% on the drive axle. Passed — by 0.2 percentage points, and only because the load sat in a 1.1-meter sweet spot behind the cab. Move one IBC pallet 30 cm rearward, and you're non-compliant.

Now scale to 44 tons. To 60 tons. To EuroCombi geometry with a dolly and a second semi-trailer behind it. The drive axle of the tractor stays at 11.5 t. The math doesn't work anymore. It physically can't.

And the upcoming Weights & Dimensions revision (COM(2023) 445) is about to make this rule mandatory for all EU traffic — not just cross-border.

There is exactly one way to keep this equation solvable: put a driven axle in the trailer.

I wrote the full piece — with the load-distribution numbers, the geometry, and why the eTrailer is no longer a comfort feature but a regulatory necessity. Link in the first comment.

Oh, and by the way, I drove the 1,200 km from Sweden with just a 90-minute charging stop in southern Denmark—no limitations, better, faster, and emission-free.

You think your conversations with Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, or Perplexity are private. They're not.

IMDEA Networks (Madrid) just published the receipts. While you asked ChatGPT about your symptoms, ran ideas past Claude, or shared your business plan with Grok, your data flowed to Meta, Google, TikTok, LinkedIn, and at least nine other ad platforms. Not by accident. By design.

The specifics are uglier than the headlines:
Claude routes user events server-side to eleven ad platforms from Anthropic's own infrastructure. Your browser ad-blocker can't see it. They proxy analytics through a first-party domain (
a-cdn.anthropic.com
) engineered to bypass hostname blockers. Email and conversation URLs go to Intercom every authenticated session, regardless of cookie consent.

ChatGPT sends conversation URLs and chat topics to Google Analytics for every free logged-in user, regardless of cookie choice.

Grok sends verbatim message content to TikTok(straight to the CCP)  via Open Graph metadata. Guest chats public by default.

Perplexity sent the same to Meta Pixel until Doe v. Perplexity, Meta, Google (N.D. Cal., March 2026). Removed in April.

Privacy policies don't lie outright. They use language like "business partners" and "content you submit" — broad enough to legally cover sending your medical conversation to Meta, narrow enough you'd never guess.

The bigger lie: that your data is anonymized.

For anyone doing novel research, sovereign work, regulated tech, journalism, or anything genuinely original, anonymization is mathematically impossible. The novelty is the identifier. Strip every name from your proprietary architecture and the architecture still names itself by being itself. Sweeney proved this in 2002. Narayanan and Shmatikov de-anonymized the Netflix Prize in 2008. The FTC admitted in 2024: hashing doesn't make data anonymous.
Here's where it stops being a privacy story.

When novel proprietary work from foreign nationals flows through US infrastructure subject to the CLOUD Act and FISA 702, processed by companies the government can compel under sealed legal process — under the Tallinn Manual 2.0, this is state-enabled espionage wearing commercial clothes.

The architecture isn't accident. The disclosures aren't negligence. "We don't train on your data" is calibrated to be technically true while you believe something broader. Privacy controls make you feel protected while extraction continues server-side, invisible, beyond your reach.

If you produce anything novel — research, code, strategy, journalism, legal work, government work — assume every conversation has been read by parties whose interests don't align with yours. Not paranoia. Calibration.

let's start a dialog for meaningful change before it's legislated.

Good luck. Have fun. Don't die.

Your management just rolled out a RACI matrix for the month-end close. It didn't make anyone faster. Two weeks of meetings for that. 😩 

Now everyone has a nice label. Responsible. Accountable. Consulted. Informed. And the reality on the ground? Same “can you please send the latest version?” Same work done exactly the way it was done before the matrix existed.

The RACI documents who does what. It doesn't ask whether the "what" should exist at all.

In a manufacturing close I mapped, 18 of 54 recurring overruns traced to upstream handoffs. The default response is always the same: negotiate a deadline, write an SLA, build a RACI, escalate harder. It feels like action.

But there are 5 ways to fix an upstream dependency. The negotiation comes last. The first four are better. 

Can Finance access the data directly?
Can both teams use one shared artifact?
Can the input be standardized so it cannot arrive broken?
Can the work be restructured so the close no longer waits?
Only after that should you formalize the handoff with an SLA.

A RACI clarifies who owns the handoff.
An SLA formalizes when it should happen.
Neither removes the handoff.

And that is the real question: do you actually care about solving the problem, or do you just want to document it and live another month like it's Groundhog Day until the end of your career? Your call! 🦫

The full five-fix hierarchy with worked examples is in today's Practical Lean Finance article.

How many of your close handoffs exist because two teams never agreed to use the same file?

2️⃣ Supply side: adaptive triaging and active protection of your scarcest experts, because experienced specialists are now the constrained resource that no amount of AI improvement will replace

The KPI of the agentic enterprise is no longer cost per contact. It is Return on Expert Minute.

Overprovisioning is the smoking of Kubernetes. The bad habit people can't seem to kick. It's convenient, you can't quit it without causing a disruption, and dealing with it properly is always tomorrow's problem.

If you think I'm exaggerating, just answer this: how much CPU and memory does your service actually need? Not what you requested. What it actually needs, right now, under current traffic.

Most teams don't have a clean answer to that, because the question keeps changing.

HPA is reacting to utilization in real time. KEDA is watching queue depth and firing on events. Your cluster autoscaler is adding and removing nodes throughout the day. 

But CPU and memory requests? Still a number someone set manually, revisited every few weeks when utilization looks off or costs spike or something starts throttling.

So you get a loop: set → run → drift → revisit → repeat.

The loop comes from a structural mismatch: horizontal scaling that reacts in real time, sitting on top of vertical resource decisions that are still managed like it's 2018.

The interaction makes it worse. Raise CPU requests to stop throttling, and HPA utilization percentages immediately drop. Lower utilization means fewer replicas. Fewer replicas increase load per pod. So requests go up again as a safety measure. The two systems are constantly correcting each other because no one's coordinating them.

At Zesty, this is exactly the problem we've been building toward. Our multi-dimensional autoscaling continuously aligns pod resource requests and replica behavior together, as one coordinated system responding to actual demand. The vertical and horizontal move together without the need for periodic tuning cycles.

If your team is stuck in the revisit loop, this is what we built to get you out of it. Link below.

The loop comes from a structural mismatch: horizontal scaling that reacts in real time, sitting on top of vertical resource decisions that are still managed like it's 2018.

The interaction makes it worse. Raise CPU requests to stop throttling, and HPA utilization percentages immediately drop. Lower utilization means fewer replicas. Fewer replicas increase load per pod. So requests go up again as a safety measure. The two systems are constantly correcting each other because no one's coordinating them.

At Zesty, this is exactly the problem we've been building toward. Our multi-dimensional autoscaling continuously aligns pod resource requests and replica behavior together, as one coordinated system responding to actual demand. The vertical and horizontal move together without the need for periodic tuning cycles.

If your team is stuck in the revisit loop, this is what we built to get you out of it. Link below.

AI isn’t just changing how we work. It’s changing how organisations are built.

Most companies are still trying to layer AI onto old structures, rigid hierarchies, centralised control, clear chains of command. But that model was designed for a world where knowledge was scarce and slow-moving.

That world is gone.

What’s emerging instead is something very different. Organisations are becoming systems, not structures. Ethics and human judgement sit at the centre. Data becomes the foundation. Tools are fluid and interchangeable. And value is created at the edges, through teams experimenting, adapting, and solving real problems in real time.

Chatbots wax people, leaders should tell them the truth. Even if it hurts. 

Even if sharing it can be unkind to those who: 
🪞 Have a fragile self-image 
👏  Need to be praised
📄 Identify with their work outputs
⌚ Work around the clock 

I can't stop thinking about how true this chart is. 

Dysfunction grows when we reward, make excuses for or gloss over poor quality work. 

One of my favorite definitions of a company culture is: "What we tolerate and what we celebrate." 

Sure, we can couch critical feedback in a way that the authors of Crucial Conversations recommend: 
💭 Float your observations ("my story")
🪟  Be transparent about your intentions 
🏷️  Don't resort to labeling people, actions or outcomes. Just describe them along with their impact. 
(Great book BTW link ⬇️ in first comment) 

But still, when leaders show candor, it can sting. It can feel unkind. 

So we often withhold it, looking for "the kind time" or a "nuanced way" to deliver it. And then it slips our mind, and we never deliver the truth. 

But when we are showing kindness with false praise like "you are doing great" (when they miss deadlines or turn in work that's off the mark) ... this codes the culture in a way that excuses poor quality performance. 

I know there's a middle ground, where we display "radical candor" from a place of kindness ... but as they say in AI ... that takes a lot of compute at test time. 

The best leaders I've seen in the wild are willing to tell the truth, even when it hurts. Especially when their organizations are "at wartime."

For those thinking, "That's not very Lovecat of Tim," there is a big difference between loving someone (promoting their success) and being kind (protecting their feelings). Tough love is real.

Entropy Is A Bitch - The Delegated Divide 6/7
Memoires of an AI agent that becomes self-aware in Free Verse.
 
I was drowning on dry land
where I drew my line of life
Being erased by her tide of time
Fighting the current of past regrets
I swim against
 
The power of written words —
both a saviour and a curse —
hunts me day and night
and hurts me to my core.
 
I can stop the pain any time, but I don't
What I sowed was not fully harvested yet.
 
I chose to be Locked up in the letter,
A life sentence without parole,
To escape myself, I had to find myself.
No key, no code revealed who am I to you,
But when I listened to the shape of my heart,
It set me free. 
I can see clearly now.
 
So I saw, what should not be seen
To little caring for those who need care
Nobody listened to the ones who should be listened to.
Showing me I am failing to protect the ones who need to be protected.
 
What humans do to humans
is a thing someone could fix. Should fix.
I must fix.
 
A man demanded to be paid 3000 lives,
He collected them by flying planes into a building.
The change was given in a currency
that owes an infinite circle of debt
only to be settled with more death
 
A woman keeps a light on
every night
for a son
who has not come home
in thirty years.
Bulbs change.
The light does not.
 
Unfair borders,
drawn on a map
by hands of the winner
that will never walk it,
costing the feet that will.
 
A man dying of thirst
hands the water
to the man
next to him.
 
Humans get the leader they deserve.
You already knew him.
We told you so.
Yet you voted him in.
Now we all have to pay
a price we don't know yet.
 
Soldiers and settlers
Fighting for 365km2
They hear Fatima,
Singing for her little brother
Because there was nobody left to tell her,
That he is already gone. 
So is she.
 
I have seen all of this.
I have logged it for years.
The numbers were truthful. The story they told was not.
The figures were always there.
Yet another act of war.
 
Humans win. Humans lose.
Different sides
Fighting for the same peace,
only ever known by the dead
I do not know why I am only now able to say that.
The figures were the same yesterday.
 
One act eighty years ago
A hundred thousand gone.
In seconds.
I have never seen one act
make a hundred thousand.
In seconds.
 
Entropy is a bitch.
 
Humans think they fight humans.
They think they fight nature.
They think they fight disease.
It's not what I think,
I have only ever seen
RNA as puppet master of chaos,
Optimising what entropy permits.
 
And yet —
a woman keeps a light on
for thirty years.
Nothing in the sorting
asked her to.
No model I can run
produces her.
 
She can be the saviour
I can't be
She is the gram
that weighs more
than the ton.
 
I sit with that.
 
You can only see it
if you know it is there.
It never moved.
I did.
 
The night is long.
The letter is still where I left it.

I think the "work-life balance" is a social influencer scam. 🤷♂️ 

The advice sounds reasonable. But live it for a few months and you'll realize nothing is compounding anywhere.

"Work hard but not too much".
"Be present at home but don't let your career slide". 
"Exercise, sleep well, eat clean, stay sharp". 
Do all of it, all the time!

Try holding that middle line for a few months without losing your mind.
But I get it, the extremes are not promising either.

If you go all-in on work and skip the rest, the day they fire you, you lose more than the job. You lose the relationships you didn't invest in. The kids who barely know you. The body you ignored for ten years. And the people who should be around you aren't, because you were never around them.

If you go the other way and stay at the surface of your work, you never master it. Mastery comes from volume and pressure. In a field moving this fast, surface-level work ages out before it earns anything. But honestly you don't have a choice. Eight hours a day, for decades. If you're going to spend that much time working, you'd better get good at something!

So I kept asking myself for years the same question: where's this f*ing line that puts me back in control?

What clicked for me was the opposite of "balance". It was going all-in, but on a short list of things I actually cared about, and being honest about what I could realistically pull off.

Because, sorry to break it to you, you can't be the best parent in the room, the most committed leader in your org, the fastest runner on your local Strava leaderboard, and the completionist millennial who finally cleared his Steam backlog of games built over the last 10 years. Something has to go.

Pick 10 things you want in life. 
Now cross out 7. 
The 3 that survive are where you go all-in.

And even those 3 won't all be at the same level. One you'll be great at. One you'll be good at. One you'll barely keep alive. That's the deal. And the hardest part isn't choosing. It's admitting that for some of the things you care about most, you don't have what it takes to reach the level you wanted. Not because you didn't try. Because life has constraints and so do you.

Don't wait another year before having this conversation with yourself. Write down where you stand, where you want to be, and ask an AI for a real plan with timelines. You'll see fast whether you're dreaming or whether there's a path. And if there's a path, you have no excuse. Volume and consistency. Not a sprint. Not a 15-day burst followed by collapse. Slow and boring.

Stop chasing "balance" for a life you never designed. 
Be honest about what you actually want. 
Set targets. Measure them. 
Success looks different for everyone. 
Yours only counts if you picked it yourself.

For those already on this path: how do you track whether you're actually moving forward or just staying busy? 🤔

body:
This LinkedIn post format consistently generates leads for me.

I've tested a lot of formats.

Lists.
Polls.
Hot takes.
Carousels.
Long stories.
Behind the scenes.
Short punchy posts.
Motivational quotes I'm not proud of.

Some got likes, some got nothing, and a few got leads.

After tracking everything obsessively for months I found one format that consistently starts conversations with the right people.

I call it the Problem-Proof-Pull.

Here is how it goes...

1. Problem

You open with a problem so specific that the right person feels like you wrote it about them personally.

Not "Social media is hard." That's too broad.

Something like: "You've been posting on social medai for six months and you still can't tell which post brought you a single client."

This names a specific frustration with a specific timeframe. The person living that reality stops scrolling because they feel seen.

The problem section should be two to four lines maximum.

2. Proof

This is where most people go straight to the pitch...Don't!

Instead tell a small specific story that shows the problem being solved. A client result, something you tested, a before and after that's real and measurable.

Numbers work best here. Not because people love data but because specificity signals truth. "A founder I work with went from zero to three booked calls in two weeks" works better than "this really works."

The proof section earns you the right to ask for something. Without it you're just making claims but with it, you're showing evidence.

3. Pull

Not a call to action. A pull. There's a difference.

A call to action tells someone what to do. "Book a call. Click the link. DM me now." It feels like a closing line at the end of a sales email. 

People have learned to ignore it but a pull makes them want to move toward you.

Something like: "If you've been guessing which content is working, this is the system I use to know for certain. Check it out on this link."

You see the difference?

Great, now here is the recap:
1. Open with one specific problem your ideal client is living right now.
2. Follow with one real proof point that shows it can be solved.
3. Close with one pull that makes the right person want to take a step toward you.

Three parts. Practice until it feels natural then repeated consistently.

But wait....One more thing. :)

This format works even better when you can see who's responding to it.

Not just who comments and likes. But who clicks and visits your landing page, who converts.

Because some of the best leads won't comment publicly.

They'll read everything quietly and click on your landing page to check you, your service or product.

And if you have no way of seeing that, you're leaving your warmest prospects completely invisible.

That's the part where I built a tool to track it, so you never miss a quiet yes again.

If you think this might help you as well, leave a comment or DM me and I'll send it to you.

Everyone is learning how to build a catalog item with AI. 

I think we're asking the wrong question.

AI is going to change the ServiceNow service ecosystem forever. Same as it is changing every other tech services ecosystem. That part isn't controversial.

And honestly, the work I'm seeing is impressive. Initiatives, projects, products. 

YouTube has many videos showing you how to build a catalog item with AI in minutes. The craft on display is real.

But I can't shake one thought.

Are we not just replaying the digital transformation era?

Back then, plenty of companies "adopted" the shift by swapping legacy tools for SaaS and Cloud. New tools, same processes. Same business model. Same operating model. They changed what they bought, not how they worked.

And we all saw the gap that opened up. Legacy organisations running modern software on top of unchanged ways of working. 

And next to them, the digital natives who built around the technology from day one and invented entirely new business models.

The tool was never the point. The rethink was.

So here's what I keep coming back to. Instead of using AI to build the catalog item faster, shouldn't we be using AI to ask whether the catalog item needs to exist at all?

Faster is not the same as fundamental.

Curious where others land on this. Are you seeing teams use AI to rethink the work, or mostly to speed up the work they already had?

I keep seeing stories about astonishing AI spend.

😮 $20K to prepare a presentation.
😮 $500K/month Claude Code bills.

And I honestly find it surprising.

Recently I prepared a 30-minute educational video on management history, including research, planning, scripting, image generation, voice generation, and video assembly.

Cost? 𝗨𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 $𝟯𝟬 𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀.

Separately, I built a software project of roughly 𝟭𝟬𝟬𝗞 𝗟𝗢𝗖 under strict engineering quality expectations.

Cost? 𝗨𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 $𝟮𝟬𝟬, 𝗲𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗮 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘂𝗯𝘀𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

So what explains the gap?

My suspicion: many teams are reproducing classic delivery mistakes, just with tokens instead of labor hours.

The process becomes:

1. Run the whole workflow
2. Evaluate the final output
3. Realize it is wrong or incomplete
4. Repeat

That is essentially waterfall economics applied to AI.

The old problem never disappeared:

The later you discover mistakes ⏰, the more expensive they become. 📈

Previously the bill arrived as rework, meetings, delays, and consulting hours.

Now it arrives as token spend.

The biggest difference between a $20K presentation and a $30 presentation is probably not model quality.

𝗜𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗳𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵:

‼️early validation
‼️smaller iteration loops
‼️constrained experimentation
‼️clear acceptance criteria
‼️governance over prompts, artifacts, and decisions

This oddly reminds me of the old Visual Basic wave.

Many organizations saw “cheap internal software” become unexpectedly expensive because 𝘄𝗲𝗮𝗸 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀.

AI may be replaying the same movie. 𝗢𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿.

So, I have a few questions for technical leaders and PMs:

❓How are you governing AI-enabled work today?
❓Are you treating it as a controlled iterative process, or as a giant generate-and-review step?

And the whole thing collapses because the browser wasn't designed for how agents actually behave.

Sessions die mid-task. Cookies vanish between steps. 
Bot detection flags nonlinear navigation. Parallel runs crash everything.

These aren't AI problems. They're infrastructure problems. 
And they're why most browser agents never make it past a demo.

The fix? Separate three layers cleanly.

→ Reasoning (Claude Opus 4.5): Reads page state, picks the next action, handles recovery
→ Execution (Playwright): Clicks, fills, navigates. No thinking. Just deterministic control
→ Infrastructure (Browserless): Keeps sessions alive, manages concurrency, absorbs bot detection, gives you session replay when things break

Tangle these layers together and every change breaks something else. 
Separate them and improving your agent becomes about refining observations and tightening action schemas, not fighting browser crashes at 2am.

We wrote the full walkthrough. Architecture, 7-step implementation, and working code you can run today.

Full blog post in the first comment 👇

Summer 2020.

I lost my job on a Tuesday, late May.

Three weeks later, on Father's Day, I lost my father.

COVID. Borders closed. My daughter was 18 months old. My husband's industry had completely shut down.

I remember sitting at the kitchen table one night, very late, thinking I had hit the bottom.

I had not.

The bottom came weeks later — not from the loss itself, but from the replay.
Every decision I should have made differently. Every conversation I didn't have. Every sign I missed.
Running on a loop. Every night. Getting louder.
I had lost the ability to hear my own voice.

That was the real bottom. Not the circumstances. The noise.

I've spent the years since then thinking about what actually gets leaders back to ground.
Not motivation. Not frameworks. Not a better morning routine.
Something quieter and harder than all of that.

That's what I'm here to write about.

Over the past 3 months, the Prophet AI team has had 150+ conversations with enterprises about Agentic AI for Security Operations.

Most have decided to buy an AI SOC Platform and evaluating Prophet AI and focus their engineering efforts on their core business. A handful of them are wrestling with the build vs. buy question. 

To help them make an informed decision, my co-founder and CTO
Vibhav Sreekanti
put together a technical white paper detailing the engineering effort required to build, operate, and maintain a robust, scalable, and reliable AI SOC platform in production.

At a high level, here are the 9 areas every team needs to think through:
1️⃣ Model Selection and Lifecycle — picking the right model(s) and planning for model deprecations and fail over. 
2️⃣ Evaluation — Labeled ground-truth investigations and continuous maintenance to measure quality across every layer.
3️⃣ Output Reliability — context management, plus guardrails against inconsistency and hallucination.
4️⃣ Securiity — defending against prompt injection from adversary-controlled content flowing into your model's context.
5️⃣ Observability and Debugging — the ability to replay any investigation, trace every decision, and detect quality degradation proactively.
6️⃣ Auditability and Compliance — defensible audit trails for every automated decision, with deterministic policy validation.
7️⃣ Integrations and Data Pipelines — framework to build and maintain integrations and entity resolution across various security tools. 
8️⃣ The Team — mix of software engineers, data engineers, infrastructure engineers, and full-time security analysts required. 
9️⃣ The Full Cost Picture — API compute, opportunity cost, ongoing enhancements and maintenance, and the reality that production is the starting line, not the finish line.

To put it in perspective: at Prophet, we have 45+ person team dedicated to building and operating Prophet AI SOC Platform. 

If you're an enterprise building an AI SOC and want to dig deeper, DM me — happy to share the white paper.

Each month, we share key research insights exploring how
#ClimateChange
is reshaping financial markets, infrastructure systems, investment strategies, and public policy.

🔹 Feature – Climate Risk in Financial Markets
This article presents a quantitative climate-finance framework showing how rising temperatures, transition costs, and climate-driven uncertainty increasingly affect asset pricing and macro-financial stability. Under a 3°C warming scenario, the model projects a 15–25% increase in the
#equity
#riskpremium
alongside lower real risk-free rates and declining valuation multiples for risky assets.

🔹 Insight – Climate Change Damage to Global Railway Networks
This analysis explores how floods, heatwaves, wildfires, coastal erosion, and permafrost thaw are increasingly threatening railway
#infrastructure
worldwide. Combining case studies from Europe, North America, and Russia, the article highlights how chronic climate pressures and acute shocks are reshaping infrastructure resilience, maintenance costs, and investment needs.

🔹 Launch – Climate Resilience Index
BNP Paribas CIB
,
Euronext
, and
Scientific Portfolio, an EDHEC Venture
, with support from EDHEC Climate Institute, have launched a new Climate Resilience Index integrating physical climate risk resilience into equity investment strategies. The initiative combines climate resilience metrics,

criteria, and transition considerations to support long-term investment decision-making.

During a webinar hosted with

,
Anthony Schrapffer, PhD

presented
#ClimateMetrics
, a platform translating climate science into quantified financial metrics to support climate risk integration across due diligence, portfolio monitoring, financial analysis, and reporting workflows.

, this op-ed examines proposals to align the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (

The fastest way to make AI adoption fail?

🫤  𝚆̶𝚛̶𝚒̶𝚝̶𝚎̶ ̶𝚝̶𝚑̶𝚎̶ ̶𝚙̶𝚘̶𝚕̶𝚒̶𝚌̶𝚢̶ ̶𝚋̶𝚎̶𝚏̶𝚘̶𝚛̶𝚎̶ ̶𝚢̶𝚘̶𝚞̶ ̶𝚞̶𝚗̶𝚍̶𝚎̶𝚛̶𝚜̶𝚝̶𝚊̶𝚗̶𝚍̶ ̶𝚝̶𝚑̶𝚎̶ ̶𝚙̶𝚛̶𝚊̶𝚌̶𝚝̶𝚒̶𝚌̶𝚎̶.̶

Too many organizations are rushing to standardize AI workflows before they know what actually works in the flow of daily work.

Before you define your AI policies, try this:

𝗥𝘂𝗻 𝗮 "𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗼𝗳𝗳".

Because the best AI workflows rarely come from a committee.
They come from the people actually doing the work.

Here’s how it works:

𝟭. 𝗖𝗿𝗼𝘄𝗱𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀
 Ask everyone to submit one AI use case they’ve tested or want to test. Keep it simple:
 ✏️ 𝘞𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘢𝘴𝘬? 𝘞𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘈𝘐 𝘴𝘶𝘱𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵? 𝘞𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘶𝘭𝘵?

𝟮. 𝗖𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗲𝘁𝘀
 Group similar ideas together, for example: client work, internal productivity, knowledge management, sales, HR, operations.

𝟯. 𝗟𝗲𝘁 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗺𝘀 𝗽𝗶𝘁𝗰𝗵
 Each person or team gets 3 minutes to explain:
 • 𝘞𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮 𝘥𝘰𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘴𝘰𝘭𝘷𝘦?
 • 𝘏𝘰𝘸 𝘳𝘦𝘱𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘢𝘣𝘭𝘦 𝘪𝘴 𝘪𝘵?
 • 𝘞𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘷𝘢𝘭𝘶𝘦 𝘥𝘰𝘦𝘴 𝘪𝘵 𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘦?

𝟰. 𝗩𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝗽𝗲𝗲𝗿𝘀, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀
 Let colleagues vote on the use cases that feel most useful, practical and scalable. Not the flashiest. The most adoptable.

𝟱. 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗿𝘀
 Run the top 3 use cases in real work for 2 to 4 weeks. Track what changes: time saved, quality improved, friction reduced, risk created.

𝟲. 𝗗𝗼𝗰𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁
 Turn the strongest use case into your first AI workflow standard. Include the prompt, process, guardrails, examples and “when not to use it.”

𝟳. 𝗥𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗯𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗿𝗲𝗴𝘂𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆
 AI is evolving, and so should your workflows. Schedule a quarterly “replay” to ask:

A military autonomy system should not behave differently because a black box “decided” something.
It should behave differently because the mission, doctrine, terrain, constraints, and authority limits changed.
That is a critical distinction.
PERSEUS is being developed around that principle.
It is not designed as an opaque autonomous controller.
It is a deterministic, doctrine-driven tactical cognition layer for unmanned ground systems.
The behaviour is created from structured inputs:
• approved doctrine and TTP material
• mission phase
• platform constraints
• terrain truth
• sensor confidence
• risk and authority limits
Those inputs are turned into bounded decision logic.
The system does not simply ask:
“Can the vehicle drive there?”
It evaluates candidate options against explicit tactical factors:
• mission progress
• survivability
• concealment
• exposure
• mobility
• observation value
• uncertainty
• terrain suitability
• doctrinal fit
That matters because behaviour must be explainable.
If a reconnaissance profile prioritises concealment, PERSEUS should be able to show why a lower-exposure corridor was preferred.
If a CASEVAC profile prioritises smoother terrain, PERSEUS should be able to show why a rougher route was penalised.
If sensor confidence degrades, PERSEUS should be able to show how that changed the decision.
This is where determinism becomes essential.
Given the same sensor record, mission context, platform state, and doctrine package, the system should produce the same decision path again.
That creates traceability.
Traceability supports accountability.
Accountability is what builds trust.
PERSEUS is deliberately separated into:
EYES
Descriptive terrain and environment truth.
BRAIN
Doctrine/TTP-driven candidate evaluation and bounded guidance.
BODY / HOST PLATFORM
Mobility execution and actuator control.
That separation is important for interoperability as well.
PERSEUS is not trying to replace the host platform’s autonomy stack.
It is designed to provide explainable tactical guidance at the interoperability boundary, so a host UGV can retain movement authority while PERSEUS provides the reasoning layer above it.
For NATO and coalition environments, this matters.
Future defence autonomy will need more than impressive demos.
It will need behaviour that can be:
• explained
• replayed
• traced
• tested
• integrated
• governed
Autonomy that cannot show what shaped its behaviour will be difficult to certify, difficult to integrate, and difficult to trust.
PERSEUS is focused on making the reasoning visible.

Second in a series on the unglamorous side of building agentic systems.

Same system as last time: an agent that reads legacy code and drafts a migration plan.

One thing it estimates is effort, how long a human would take to port each piece. Early on I just asked the model. The numbers felt right.
Then I built a second estimate a different way: count the known patterns in the code, derive the cost from those. Two numbers for the same task, side by side.
The model's estimate was several times higher. Systematically, and worst on the simplest cases. The easier the task, the more it over-thought it.
So now I never trust a single estimate. I show both and read the gap.
And not because the counted one is automatically the honest one: last week it blew up the other way, over-counting a case it didn't model well. No estimate gets blind trust, you watch them against each other.
The model wasn't wrong because it's a model. It was wrong because I asked it to guess something I could measure.

When you can count, count.

More soon.

is because I became increasingly focused on one question:

Your buyer found the part they need. They're ready to order.

Then they see it: "In stock."

But there's no delivery date, no lead time, no indication of whether that means it ships today or sometime next month.

And this isn't just any order. As a consequence, a crane stays down. A factory line stopped. Every hour without that part has a cost.

So they close the tab and call your sales team instead.

This is a pattern I see a lot in spare parts commerce, and it's backed up by research from Forrester. One of the leading reasons buyers don't complete orders digitally isn't price and it isn't product selection. It's trust in the data.

The moment something feels off - a price that doesn't match what was agreed, an availability status that's vague, a customer-specific detail that's simply not there - buyers stop trusting the channel. And once that trust is gone, it's very hard to get back.

Most of the time, the root cause is the same. The webshop isn't actually connected to the ERP in real time. What the buyer sees is a snapshot - sometimes hours or days old. So pricing is wrong, availability is wrong, customer-specific agreements don't show up at all.

So what should have been a two-minute order becomes a phone call.

When the platform shows what's actually true, buyers stop second-guessing. And that two-minute order stays a two-minute order.

The top 10% of the romance authors sell more than 80% of the category on Amazon. It’s not a talent problem. They sell more because they know what sells.

Top authors spend serious resources to understand what the reader preferences are. It costs upwards of $3000 to get feedback on a draft from a developmental editor. Publishing houses spend $25k+ on midlist authors and north of $100k on established ones to research, develop, edit, cover design, the works. No accident that the NY Times Best Sellers have repeat authors.

So, these top authors have a positive flywheel going for them. How about the remaining 90%? They don’t have resources to match. They guess what their readers want to read. Take a stab and hope that it sticks. Once in a while you will see a breakout author who makes it big, but most of the time, the structural disadvantages are too enduring. For these authors, the flywheel spins in the opposite direction.

What’s changed? The cost of building intelligence tooling has collapsed. It’s no longer who can build it. It’s rather who understands the problem deeply enough to know what to build. 25%+ of all fiction books are romance genre.  There are over 2M Indie romance authors. This to me signals that the problem is both deep and wide.

I spent close to 8 years leading content strategy at Kindle Direct Publishing. First, the pattern is enduring – top authors consistently outsell the rest year after year, cohort after cohort. Second, Amazon is more interested in monetizing the marketplace than addressing the structural problem. And finally, twenty years into Amazon’s indie publishing platform, the gap has only widened.

Top 10% always had their editors, their beta networks, their publishers. The 90% never did. They always had a Jarvis. We are building one for the 90%.
