Brands don't get to choose between scale and accuracy. They need both.

The assumption that precision belongs to small batch work doesn't survive contact with how modern brands actually operate. A logo has to be exact on the tenth asset and the ten thousandth. Embroidery has to read the same way every time. Anything less isn't usable.

Generative AI has a real weakness here. You produce an image, one detail is off, you regenerate, a different detail breaks. Round and round. For brand teams, that loop is the thing that quietly kills the business case for AI content production. The token bill grows, the calendar slips, and the output still isn't right.

Detail Fixer is our answer to that.

In the video I show how it works end to end. Hover, select the area that needs correcting, and the artifact from your original input replaces it directly. No second guessing the model. The thing you uploaded is the thing that shows up.

It doubles as an editing tool too. When the lighting and background are exactly where you want them but a specific detail isn't carrying through, Detail Fixer pulls it forward without disturbing the rest of the frame.

We built it first for logos. Then, in close collaboration with our partners, we opened it up to other AI weak points, text, clothing details like buttons / zippers and more. 

Plenty more on the roadmap. Follow along, or get in touch if you want to see it up close

i've watched dozens of funded founders post their announcement on linkedin in the last year.

almost all of them shipped the same post. almost all of them lit the moment on fire.

the funding round is the most attention you'll get in 18 months. and most founders use that window to write the post their cap table wants to read, not the one their customer needs to see.

the standard fundraise post hits five beats:

performative gratitude. investor tag dump. coffee-shop origin story. "we're hiring, DM me." a row of hashtags at the end.

your buyer has seen this exact post two hundred times this quarter. you've lost them by line three.

the post your customer actually needs answers three questions instead.

→ what changes for them. funding doesn't make your product better today — it makes you more likely to exist at renewal. say that directly. 
your enterprise buyers are reading this asking one question: will these people still be around when our contract comes up?

→ what you're building next, specifically. not "expanding the team and accelerating the roadmap." name the wedge. name the problem you're solving in the next six months that you couldn't solve last week.

→ what stays the same. the buyer's real fear isn't that you'll fail. it's that you'll change. tell them which decisions you'll keep making personally. tell them what you refuse to outsource even at scale.

the founders who post the standard announcement get likes from other founders.

the founders who post the second kind get DMs from customers asking what's coming next.

guess which one matters in 18 months.

Most RL systems are passive about their own classification scheme. They classify, then act. The action gets reviewed only if a human happens to notice it was wrong.

For request-response agents this works. The user is the ground truth. They complain if something is wrong (if they notice).

For continuously running agents, this fails. And it fails in a specific way worth noticing.

We built an attention triage layer for our always-on entities. It worked. Signals flowed through, reflexes learned, dashboards stayed green. Magnificent to look at. 

Then a user sent "you sent it to the wrong Michael" (a pretty significant correction about a real operational failure) and the reflex layer absorbed it as routine chatter. The entity never saw it... 

The reflex's confidence ticked up because absorption with no complaint reads, to the learner, as success.

Hello to a new category: Operational blindness. 

The system had so successfully compressed its own input that anomalies were indistinguishable from noise.

The fix is small: ε-greedy from the bandit literature. 5% of signals that would be absorbed get through anyway. The system always carries a live sample of what its categories exclude.

This way, the pattern becomes bigger than the fix.

An agent that doesn't probe its own categories will eventually go blind to the things its categories don't see. 

Remember, these are not deterministic robots. 

The failure modes of continuous agents are not the failure modes of supervised learning. They are closer to the failure modes of organisms, i.e. Confident, well-adapted, and quietly miscalibrated to a world that has shifted under them.

Lost in Translation: Part 1

People often ask me what I actually do….I’m a translator 

R&D engineers are masterminds at solving technical problems.Marketers are brilliant at building creative stories people care about.

But these two worlds do not always translate cleanly into each other.

That is where technology marketing often gets lost. You usually end up with one of two things.

A campaign that is technically accurate, but too product-led. Or a campaign that is creative, but so light on detail that the product could be almost anything.

The job is to sit in the middle.

Let me show you what I mean.

I recently saw this washing machine campaign about AI. If you read between the lines, you can almost hear the meeting that took place underneath it.

Engineer: The AI uses multiple sensors and algorithms to adjust and optimise the wash.

Marketer: Sounds smart. Give me an example.

Engineer: One sensor monitors how the clothes move in the drum.

Marketer: Why?

Engineer: To wash the clothes optimally 

Marketer: ….Leave it with me.

But there is a better story underneath.

This is not just a washing machine with AI.

It’s a self driving washing machine that can measure things like load weight, fabric movement and how dirty the water is. Then it can adjust the wash as it runs, instead of treating every load like a fixed programme. Ultimately without making you decode every setting.

That is the story.

if I had to turn it into a campaign line:

The self-driving washing machine.
Power on. Take it for a spin.

Is that perfect? Probably not.

But it gets much closer to the value.

Because people do not buy “fabric behaviour detection.”

They buy less mental space on laundry. 

Less second-guessing. Less hassle. Less worry about choosing the wrong setting and ruining clothes.

The sensors, algorithms and technical architecture still matter. They are the reason to believe.

But they should support the story, not replace it.

That is the translation challenge.

Take complex innovation. Find the human problem. Build the commercial story. Then use the technology as proof.

That is what I do.

Do you have any more examples of technology that gets lost in translation? How would you have tackled the AI washing machine ?

SLAS (Society for Laboratory Automation and Screening)
Europe 2026 in Vienna confirmed something we have been engineering toward at OpenNovations for a while: laboratory automation is past the "which robot, which liquid handler" stage. The bottleneck has moved one layer up. It is now an evidence problem.

A plate map does not explain the experiment. A worklist does not prove the transfer was feasible. A robot log does not capture scientific intent. A freezer trace does not identify which samples were exposed. Across many of the strongest sessions in Vienna, the same pattern surfaced: physical automation is well ahead of evidence automation.

That is the gap our poster presentation addressed directly. "GxP-Aligned High-Throughput Bioanalytical Automation: Chain-of-Custody, Event-Driven Data Backbone and Closed-Loop QC" presented the Aranei reference architecture as an open-source, standards-based engineering pattern for unifying laboratory automation and IT into one auditable backbone. Custody events, instrument runs, raw artifacts, data contracts, lineage, QC decisions, cybersecurity controls, and human review are not separate problems. They are one chain.

Vienna validated three positions we have been building on:

1. Open standards belong at the layers they were designed for. SiLA 2 and OPC UA LADS at the device interface. HL7, FHIR, and IHE LAW at the laboratory workflow layer. Allotrope ASM and AnIML at analytical payloads. OpenLineage for lineage. No single standard solves the whole problem; together they reduce the brittle point-to-point integration that breaks regulated labs.

2. Open-source infrastructure is the responsible default for regulated environments. Apache Kafka, PostgreSQL, Apache Airflow, Apache Iceberg, OpenLineage, GX Core, Pandera, Pydantic. A regulated customer needs to inspect, build, audit, and run the components they depend on. Source-available is not the same as open source, and the difference matters for sovereignty.

3. AI in the lab needs governed context before it needs autonomy. Agentic AI without validated workflow definitions, source-of-truth systems, and audit-ready evidence is faster ambiguity, not progress.

OpenNovations operates at these layers: systems engineering, validation support, interoperability, cybersecurity, and data integrity for regulated and high-integrity laboratory environments. If your organization is working through any of these in 2026, we should talk!

What if analytic dashboards were already dead?

That’s the widespread conversation among many data people with the fast rising of AI agents in the data & analytics domain too.

Let’s be realistic…
Although agentic AI will massively augment human capacity to rapidly analyze and extract insights, detect anomalies and identify performance shifts, we aren't throwing dashboards away entirely. In many cases, we’ll still be happy to check a good old static dashboard for locked-in, quarterly financial reporting or predictable KPI tracking while grabbing our morning coffee.

But as a mechanism for driving active business operations, real-time exploration, and answering ad-hoc questions? The executive dashboard has officially been demoted.

Instead of human teams opening up 15 different tabs, looking at static visual charts, and trying to guess the "why" behind a drop in a given KPI, business stakeholders can simply ask questions in plain English, while autonomous AI agents handle the data-layer querying behind the scenes.

But here is the silent crisis vanguard organizations are facing in production right now: AI agents don’t query data like humans do. They spin up dozens of complex, erratic, multi-step queries simultaneously. They act less like a standard software tool and more like an intense, hyper-active collaborator. 

To make this work, we have to view the agentic analytics stack in 4 distinct layers (from top to bottom):

- Context layer: Encoding operational intelligence, guardrails, and boundaries. What is the user trying to achieve right now, and what external operational context applies to this request?

- Semantic layer: It sits between raw data and the agent and deterministically translates database schemas into business definitions. (e.g., How exactly do we calculate an "activated customer" over the last 30 days?)

- Data governance (not a new friend): Human roles are shifting from execution to supervision of AI agents. It’s necessary to rethink data governance in this new paradigm. Data access, quality and lineage capabilities are key to implement secure, reliable and explainable agents.

- The Data warehouse / serving layer: The engine room. This is where the physical data actually lives, and where super-fast computation must happen.

To survive the shift from dashboard visualization to agentic analytics, you need a hyper-efficient, sub-second serving layer built natively for massive concurrency. That’s exactly why we built the Scaleway Data warehouse, powered by ClickHouse®.

will be hosting an exclusive, live technical deep-dive webinar to show you exactly how the Scaleway Data Warehouse handles these modern workloads.

I was 23 with no business plan — so I wrote one on loose leaf paper. It became my first company, TSE Sports & Entertainment.

No MBA. No fancy presentation. No investor pitch deck seeking funding. Literally a single piece of paper and a pen to write out what had been running through my head 24-7 for months.

I didn't go to business school. I didn't have a mentor handing me a template. I simply sat down and wrote out what I wanted TSE Sports and Entertainment to be. Revenue streams. Target clients. Ideas. All in my own terrible handwriting on a piece of loose leaf paper.

That was it. That was all I knew how to do. This was the plan.

I didn't even have a computer. No exaggeration. I had paper, a pen, and a phone. No letterhead, not even a logo. That's how it all started. There weren't really any hospitality companies in sports at the time. I saw an opening.

One of my first deals was an experience package for Edy's Ice Cream to the US Open Golf Tournament. That deal literally bought me the money to buy my first computer.

Before the laptop I had a fax machine. Before the fax machine came a word processor. Every sale funded the next tool. Every tool opened the next door. All the money went back into the business so I could just survive.

Nine years later, TSE was acquired by a private equity firm and became the platform company to build out one of the largest sports hospitality companies in the space at the time.

Here's what I've learned after building three companies from nothing:

People overthink the plan. They wait for the perfect deck. The perfect moment. The perfect strategy.

There is no perfect. Markets shift. Clients surprise you. What you think your business will be on day one is never exactly what it becomes.

You don't need the perfect plan.

You need a plan — and the guts to start.

Write it on a napkin. Sketch it on paper. Just get it out of your head and onto something real. Then go sell something.

The rest you'll figure out along the way.

If this business plan could lead to a successful company and a sale to a PE company, Why not you?

It's Monday morning, so much in your head of what needs to be done this week.

One of the simplest but most effective things I’ve started sharing with coaching clients is something I call The 2-Minute Reset.

Most people aren’t struggling because they’re lazy. They’re struggling because their brain 🧠 is overloaded. 

Too many thoughts.
Too many tabs open mentally.
Too many unfinished loops competing for attention.

So before making decisions, planning, or trying to “focus”, I get clients to do this:

Take any piece of paper and a pen. (Not your phone. Not your laptop.)

And for 2 minutes straight, write down EVERYTHING sitting in your head.
Tasks.
Worries.
Ideas.
Things you’re avoiding.
Conversations you need to have.
Random reminders.
Everything.

Each thing should only be 1 line, so you do not get lost in one point.

Why handwritten?

Because writing physically slows the brain down just enough to process thoughts differently. It creates separation between you and the mental noise. It creates mindfulness.

What’s interesting is that clarity usually appears before the 2 minutes is even over. And then comes the most important part:

At the bottom of the page, write ONE thing only:

👉 “What is the next task?”

Not the whole plan.
Not your 5-year strategy.
Just the next actionable step.

Because momentum is built through movement, not overthinking.

Simple.
Practical.
Surprisingly powerful.

And the best thing, it's free and can be done multiple times a day as needed.

Try it next time you feel stuck.

Your exhausted brain can't think its way out of burnout.

Winston Churchill understood this before psychology did.

He called his depression the “Black Dog.”

And when it arrived, he did something unusual.

He laid bricks.

For hours.

Brick by brick at his home in Kent until his hands hurt and his mind finally went quiet.

He even joined the bricklayers’ union.

Churchill later wrote something I think about constantly:

“People who think for a living can’t fix a tired brain by resting. They need to use a different part of themselves.”

That insight was decades ahead of its time.

Today we call it behavioral activation.

One of the most researched treatments for depression.

Because burnout creates a brutal loop:

Feel bad.
Withdraw.
Overthink.
Do less.
Feel worse.
Withdraw more.

The nervous system gets trapped in rumination.

Endless thought without resolution.

What behavioral activation does is surprisingly simple:

It interrupts the loop through action.

Not massive action.

Physical action.

Something your hands can finish.

A wall built.
A drawer organized.
A meal cooked.
A floor cleaned.
A garden planted.

Your brain gets immediate evidence that movement is still possible.

That progress is still possible.

That you're not trapped inside your own thoughts forever.

That's why physical work helps exhausted knowledge workers so much.

It temporarily pulls the brain out of abstract thinking and back into direct sensory experience.

And interestingly, the research backs Churchill up.

In a landmark University of Washington study, behavioral activation performed as well as antidepressants for severely depressed adults and outperformed talk therapy.

Which honestly makes intuitive sense.

Because sometimes the problem is not that your brain needs more analysis.

It's that your nervous system needs proof you're still capable of movement.

Most ambitious people respond to burnout by doubling down on thinking.

More podcasts.
More strategy.
More optimization.
More self-analysis.

Meanwhile their nervous system is begging for something much simpler:

Use your hands.

Build something tangible.

Create visible progress.

Get out of your head long enough for your body to remember it's safe to move again.

Even Churchill knew this:

Sometimes the most productive thing an exhausted thinker can do is stop thinking altogether.

3 pillars to customer acquisition on LinkedIn.

Most people overthink it. 50 audiences, new creatives every week, throwing money at ads that don't convert.

It comes down to three things.

1. The Hook. First line stops the scroll or nothing else matters. Your offer could be perfect. Your landing page could be flawless. Nobody will ever see it if the hook doesn't make them say "tell me more."

2. The Click-Through. This is where most ads die. Speak to their pain, not your features. One call to action. One next step. If they think "this person gets my problem," they click to the landing page. If they think "this is an ad," they scroll.

3. The Conversion. They're on your landing page. Now close. Lead with their pain. Stack social proof. And make it easy to book. Calendar embed, not a contact form. Right now, not "we'll get back to you."

Here's what most people miss. The offer matters more than the design. A clean page with a bad offer converts at zero. A simple page with a no-brainer offer prints leads.

Hook. Click-through. Conversion. Three pillars. Each one you can measure, each one you can optimize. When all three work together, LinkedIn becomes a predictable lead engine.

Here’s what to do if you're stuck under 400 impressions (i used this method to get 568,680 impressions in the last 90 days):

(This post offers only a high-level overview. If you want a full guide + video walkthrough, you can get it here free:
https://lnkd.in/d3xpVbBk
)

High-level steps:

1. Find your best performing organic post from the last 2 months. Must be either a single image, text-only, or a video. If you don’t have any outlier, just pick one. Or create a new one from scratch.

2. Go to linkedin(dot)com/ads and open an ad account if you haven’t done it before.

3. Create a new campaign. Call it TL Ads - {your name}. TL stands for “Thought Leader”. It’s an ad type we’ll use.

4. Inside this campaign, create an ad set with an Engagement objective.

5. Build your audience (don’t overthink it). Turn off Audience Expansion and LinkedIn Audience Network. If you want to be more fancy, you can upload your own accounts/contacts list. Plenty of tutorials out there.

6. In the bid section, use a Manual Bid option and set it to 30% of the suggested low bid. So if the suggested range is $1-3. Use $0.3. Start at $10-20 daily budget.

7. Click save and continue to the last step — ads.

8. Click “Browse Existing Content”. In the three tabs at the top, click “Linkedin Members” and search for your name.

9. Find 1-3 posts you want to promote and request a permission. This will generate an approval link. Open it in the next step, turn on autoapproval, and go back to the ad creation tab. Refresh.

10. Add the posts into your ad set and launch the campaign. It might ask you to add a billing method before.

And when you post something new, you can just add it into the same ad set. Or start a new campaign.

There. Reach solved for $10/day. Without spending more than 15 min here per day.

body:
Happy Monday morning 🌤️

I’ve been thinking about why texting seems to mean completely different things across generations — even within the same family.

For many of us in Gen X acknowledgement matters. We grew up in a world where communication wasn’t constant or guaranteed so when someone reached out there was usually some kind of response. Even a quick “got it” or “will reply later” felt like closing the loop rather than leaving things hanging.

Some of that comes from what our parents lived through.

My mum is only a couple of decades older than me but when she immigrated to England her main link to family in Pakistan was a thin blue aerogramme that might arrive after months of waiting and every word was cherished. My parents’ wedding ceremony was even conducted over the phone because international travel simply wasn’t realistic for many families then.

Communication was scarce and expensive so when someone reached out or responded — it felt deeply intentional and meaningful.

Fast forward to my generation: we still remember when every text cost money and international calls were a luxury so responsiveness carried emotional (and literal) weight.

Funny fact: at one point I actually had to take out a student loan partly to pay for my phone bill. Long-distance calls were not cheap. No unlimited plans. Definitely no iMessage 😂

Don’t get me wrong — I definitely don’t reply to every message immediately but I also could never peacefully live with 627 unread texts sitting there 😂

I grew up in an era where if someone didn’t respond they might literally be:
• missing
• grounded by their parents
• out of coins for the phone box
• or caught talking on the phone when they absolutely weren’t supposed to be 🤣

It was completely normal to see people my age hiding in phone boxes trying to squeeze entire conversations into a few minutes.

Meanwhile my Gen Z daughter can go hours without replying and when I finally check in, her response is often:

“It’s never that serious.” 😂

For her silence is neutral — not a sign that something is wrong just that life is happening and she’ll get to it when she can.

Same silence. Very different stories.

• Gen X brain:
“Did this disappear into the void? Did I say something wrong? Is everything okay?”

• Gen Z brain:
“They’re busy. I’ll reply when I have the energy. No big deal.”

Sometimes I wonder if this gap in how we interpret silence is one small reason so many people feel more “connected” yet lonelier than ever.

One communication style can feel thoughtful to one person and indifferent to another.

If you’re curious about the broader research on generational differences,
Jean Twenge
‘s work is a great starting point especially iGen and Generations which explore how technology and culture shape us.

So I’m curious: when someone doesn’t text back, what story do you tell yourself and where do you think that story comes from (your generation, your personality, or your experiences) ?

🔆 The reset doesn't announce itself. It just arrives.

Sometimes as a moment of clarity you weren't expecting. Sometimes as a decision that took longer than it should have but landed exactly when it needed to. Sometimes as a freezing cold swim in Brighton at 8am because someone dared you and honestly, at that point, why not.
Mine arrived as all three. 🤣 🧊 

And here's what I've learned: you're not stuck because nothing is working. You're stuck because your brain is quietly, efficiently, loyally repeating what's familiar. Same thoughts. Same reactions. Same decisions. Same life. It's not weakness: it's neuroscience. Your brain is built to protect the identity loop, not break it.

📣 The good news? You can interrupt it.

Step 1 — See the pattern. Where is your life on repeat? Not metaphorically. Actually. Write it down.
Step 2 — Interrupt the reaction. Next time the spiral starts: the overwhelm, the overthinking, the retreat into old habits; pause. One beat. That's the whole move.
Step 3 — Create daily evidence. Small actions, repeated. Not a reinvention. A recalibration.

Resilient people don't have fewer problems. They have faster reset times. Bad news at 9am. Back to priorities by 10am. The speed of the reset matters more than the size of the setback.

And if you're mid-reset and wondering if it's working: go swim in Brighton in May. It's absolutely freezing, medically questionable, and somehow resets everything the brain couldn't. 🌊❄️ 🤣 

What tipped your reset; and where did it take you?

LogiTALK

When
Kunal Maheshwari
and I sat down for
LogiTALK

LinkedIn
.

And honestly, those are usually the best conversations. The real ones.
Over the years, I have attended more network conferences than I can count. I have seen people spend thousands trying to stand out, only to be forgotten by the next event. The people you actually remember are the ones who made a genuine connection. The ones who were simply themselves.

That is something I keep telling anyone entering this industry, whether it is your first conference or your fiftieth.

❌ Do not try to sound like everyone else.
❌ Do not overthink your “personal brand.”
❌ And please do not let AI turn you into a corporate robot.

✅ People remember personality.
✅ People remember authenticity.
✅ People remember how you made them feel.

Tomorrow is National Hole in Your Bucket Day. Yeah, that's a real thing.

And before you scroll past thinking this is a deep-dive into German folk music — it's not. It's about the one number your revenue team is almost certainly lying to itself about: pipeline conversion rate.

Here's the core problem. When pipeline feels soft, the instinct is always the same: more leads. More top of funnel. More spend. More reps. More. It's Henry's logic — the bucket has a hole in it, so the answer is more water.

But the math doesn't work that way. If 90 out of every 100 leads are leaking out before they close, pouring in 200 leads doesn't fix anything. It just doubles your CAC while your conversion rate quietly holds at 10%.

The same pipeline that feels undersized is probably just underplugged. After 20+ years watching B2B companies bleed revenue, I've mapped the nine holes that show up with near-universal consistency. You have at least three. 

You probably have five.

Nine holes. Five handoff points. One folk song that perfectly explains why so many Q2 closes are already in trouble — and what to actually do about it before June.

Pull up your CRM conversion rates before you read this. The gap between where you are and where the top quartile lives is sitting right there in the data, waiting for someone to care enough to fix it.

I've been going deeper on each of these individually in recent LinkedIn posts — three down, six to go. Follow along if you want the full breakdown.

The scale of mis-selling AI in Finance is disarming. The pattern is eerily similar.

The seller opens with something true, a regulator's letter, a study, a real failure. Then they stretch that one true thing until their product is the only way out.

The bend always happens at the same joint.  Two different things get fused, so a real fact appears to prove a problem it does not actually prove.

E.g. "The model gave different answers, so you cannot audit it." 
Reproducibility and auditability are not the same thing. You audit a decision by fingerprinting it, the inputs, the model version, the human sign-off, not by making the model repeat itself.

E.g. "You have hundreds of unknown AI tools." 
Tool count is not risk. The number is a finding. The risk is which data flows where, and under whose account.
E.g. "Thirty-five million euro fine." 
The maximum penalty is not your obligation. Your obligation depends on how each system is classified.

Before the next pitch becomes a purchase, find the conflation. 

First edition of AI Trust Ledger is live, link in comments.

I attended a TEDx event in Miami a few weeks ago and left with one question I can't stop thinking about: what does consent even mean in the age of AI?

Because right now, 42% of CEOs surveyed by Yale say AI could destroy humanity within ten years. Lawsuits are being filed against OpenAI after a school shooting and a teenager's suicide. Small communities are facing water deficits because data centers are being built on their land without their input. And everyday workers are being asked to train AI models with a decade of their professional knowledge, on their normal 40-hour work week, without anyone asking if that's okay.

The printing press gave us the right to free speech. But that right didn't come with the technology. It was demanded, argued for, and built over generations.
We are in that moment right now. And the right we need to build is consent.
I am not anti AI. I am pro consent.

body:
Have you watched the show Severance? 

It's a fascinating (and unsettling) take on the idea of separating work from home (available on Apple TV). The main character enrolls in a procedure that literally splits his consciousness: when he's at work, he has zero memory of his home life, and when he's home, he has no memory of work. The different characters each have their own reasons for "severing," but the premise is the same, a hard, clean line between two worlds.

It's an interesting premise, but we are not built this way, are we? We tend to carry our ‘stuff’ around everywhere we go.

Last week I gave a lunch and learn, and during the conversation one participant made a comment that stuck with me. She said she could easily see how the lessons applied at home but wasn't as sure they translated to the workplace. I understood the hesitation, the dynamics feel different, the stakes feel different, the relationships feel different. But here's what I've come to believe deeply: the lessons don't change, the person does. The lessons can trigger profound changes in how we interact with others.

What we're really talking about is energy. Presence. Intention. The way you show up in a room before you ever say a word. Horses taught me this, they don't care about your title, your salary, or how you think you come across. 
They respond to who you actually are, in the moment. And so do people, whether they realize it or not.

So, when someone says the lessons feel more personal than professional, I'd gently push back: work teams are made up of individuals. The same person who learns to communicate with more clarity at home, who stops nagging and starts leading, who learns to ask with intention and wait for the response, that person walks into work on Monday changed. Not because they flipped a switch, but because growth doesn't stay in one room. It travels with you. What you do better at home, you do better at work.

That's why I call what I teach Whole-Life Leadership.

It's not about work-life balance. It's not about keeping two separate selves in check. It's about recognizing that the energy you carry, the way you listen, the clarity of your ask, and the presence you bring, these are not professional skills versus personal skills. They are human skills. And when you develop them, every arena of your life feels the shift.

Maybe the lessons land at home first. That's okay. Sometimes that's what needs attention first. But give it time. Change in a person doesn't stay contained. It bleeds forward: into conversations, into teams, into leadership.

You can't sever who you are. That’s a good thing, right? But we can learn to better align ourselves.

Our most forward-thinking PE partners have us building company brains at their portcos.

The reasoning is simple. The bottleneck to faster AI iteration isn't the model — it's the company's own context. Its data, its operational history, the way its best people actually make decisions, all scattered across a dozen systems+ that don't talk to each other. You can drop the smartest model in the world on top of that mess and it still can't see across the business.

So most AI work at portcos ends up as islands. A chatbot in service, a copilot in finance, a summarizer in ops. Each one re-solving the same underlying problem in isolation, none of them moving the company toward an AI-native state.

A company brain is the inversion. You unify the context once — put everything the business knows in a place an agent can reason over — and the use cases stop being a roadmap you sequence one quarter at a time. They become questions you ask. Cross-sell, claims automation, dispatch logic: not separate builds, just the same brain pointed at different problems.

Think of it like scaffolding. You put it up, and then you can actually build workflows that reach across the whole business. Without it, every project is a one-off re-solving the same access problem from scratch.

That's why some of the sharpest firms are choosing brain-first over another year of AI automation work.

There's a specific gap in life sciences AI adoption that I don't see enough people talking about. 

Enterprise AI strategies serve the C-suite. They're built for board presentations, multi-year roadmaps, and platform decisions. They answer the question "where is the company going with AI?" 

But the VP running pharmacovigilance, or medical affairs, or regulatory operations isn't asking that question. They're asking: "What does AI mean for how my team works next quarter? Which workflows change? What do I stop doing? What do I need my people to be able to do that they can't do today?" 

Enterprise strategy doesn't answer those questions. And the consulting firms selling $2M AI transformations aren't designed to answer them either, they're built for enterprise-wide engagements, not function-level operating model work. 

The result is a generation of functional leaders who are under real pressure to do something with AI and have no practical playbook for their specific department. 

That's the gap I've been spending most of my time in lately. And it's where I think the most important AI adoption work in life sciences is happening right now: not at the enterprise level, but at the function level.

This Saturday, May 30, I will turn 62

To celebrate it with my friends, colleagues and connections on LinkedIn, I am sharing some reflections on what I see regarding the Future of Work

The future of work will be won by the leaders who architect the best humans around it.

In 32 years as an executive search professional,I have watched one pattern repeat without exception: technology changes the game, but people decide who wins it.

Here are the 10 principles I now hand to every leader preparing for an AI-first decade 👇

1. Lead with a human-centered "why." 
The most respected Board Members, C-Suite Leaders, VPs and Directors I know, have a well defined "why". People nowadays and more than ever follow purpose, not profit. If your team nor your organization can't repeat your "why" in one sentence, you don't have one yet.

2. Design your organization as a learning system. 
The winners won't be the ones who restructure fastest. They'll be the ones who learn fastest. Make upskilling a weekly habit, not an annual event.

3. Hire for learning agility, not just experience. 
Static job descriptions are dying. Curiosity, resilience, and cross-functional thinking outlast any single line on a résumé.

4. Build talent ecosystems, not just teams. 
You no longer compete as a company. You compete as a node, connected to universities, bootcamps, cross-border partners, and gig talent. Access capability on demand. Stop hoarding headcount.

5. Pair AI with deep human judgment. 
AI is decision-support, not autopilot. Let it surface the patterns. Let humans own the context, the ethics, and the consequences.

6. Make skills/competencies/capacities, not roles, your currency. 
Jobs change faster than org charts. Manage capabilities, not positions, and move people fluidly to where they create the most value.

7. Treat trust and psychological safety as infrastructure. 
In Japan they call it shinrai. Innovation dies in a climate of fear. Build the rituals that reward candor and make honest failure survivable.

8. Lead across borders, cultures, and time zones. 
The most important work now happens in distributed, multicultural teams. I see it every day in the CaliBaja corridor: cross-border fluency is a strategic advantage, not an operational headache.

9. Redefine performance around outcomes. 
Presence is not performance. Measure impact and learning, not hours logged or proximity to headquarters.

10. Anchor every transformation in ethics and inclusion. 
The future of work will be judged not by what we built, but by who it served.

As you can see in all 10, every principle moves authority away from the org chart and toward the human being.

That is the real architecture of the future of work.

If you could implement ONE of these in the next 90 days, which would move your organization the most?

Drop the number in the comments. I read and reply to every one.

♻️ Save this for your next leadership offsite.

body:
In 2015, David Chang said the internet made every bowl of ramen taste the same. His argument wasn't about recipes. It was about access. Apprentices used to fail for months before they found a voice. Then the technique went online, anyone could pull a competent tonkotsu, and the variance collapsed. 

The struggle that sorted good from bad was also the thing that made people weird, and once the struggle was free, the weirdness went with it. Good ramen, everywhere, identical.

I keep coming back to it, because I'm watching AI do the same thing to slide decks.

Tonkotsu in ten seconds. Three squares, a bold bar, a title. Beautiful & the same.

There's a comforting story we tell about this. When a skill gets commoditized, differentiation doesn't die, it relocates. Anyone can make the deck now, so the contest moves up a layer, from "can you build it" to "do you have the taste to build it well." The cream still rises. It just rises higher up.

Maybe. But I don't think it's one outcome. I think it's three, and they don't compete. They stack.

1: the cream rises. Design becomes the differentiator, the people with real visual judgment pull ahead, everyone else ships the default.

2: it warps the decision first. When five vendors pitch and all five decks look machine-made, you can't read merit off the page, so you over-index on whoever looks different. The aesthetic-usability effect is real and documented (source in the comments). We trust what looks good and forgive its flaws. So the vendor who paid a human designer wins the room with the weaker offer. That's not taste rising. That's polish hijacking the call.

3: the cream doesn't rise at all. If everyone starts from the same flat default, the talented get anchored to it too, and the top drifts back toward the middle instead of pulling away.

Here's where I land. 
The sequence: pretty deck, then flattening, then recalibration, as the market clocks that "looks good" stopped meaning anything and goes hunting for the next signal. Personalization. A story. A number that holds up. Maybe no deck at all.

The split: at the very same time, the cream is rising for some people and sinking for others. Same market, same day. AI amplifies the few who already had taste and flattens everyone who was renting it from a template.

We already have a name for this in hiring. Signal inflation. When everyone can manufacture the same resume, the same cover letter, the same polished application, the signal stops meaning anything. 100s of applicants per role, most of them indistinguishable, and the thing that was supposed to tell you who's good tells you nothing.

The AI deck is signal inflation for design. Same mechanic, different surface.
So the question isn't whether AI gets better at this. It will. The question is what we reach for once "looks good" is free for everyone. When the polished version is the floor and not the ceiling, the people who win won't have the best-looking deck.

Apprentices used to fail for months before they found a voice. Then the technique went online, anyone could pull a competent tonkotsu, and the variance collapsed.

Founders who've crossed $1M and suddenly feel it's harder to sell than a year ago, your AI content has a tell.

I saw it on a coaching call w/ a Board of Directors member yesterday. Founder pulled up his last 30 LinkedIn posts. Every one of them sounded smart. Reasonable. 

Like a good agency who'd never actually run anything.

He couldn't figure out why nothing was converting.

I could.

Buyers can't name what's off. They just feel it. And it's killing your sales calls before you ever get on Zoom.

The danger isn't that your competitors publish more than you. It's that your best thinking (the stuff that took you 15 years to learn the hard way) gets sanded down by ChatGPT and reads exactly like everyone else.

Clean. Polished. Reasonable.

Forgettable as hell.

They don't say "this was written by AI." They just keep scrolling. Nobody shows up to the sales call already trusting how you think.

So you do what your content failed to do...

Explain the difference. Handle objections nobody asked. Try to install trust in 45 minutes that should've been compounding for weeks.

That's an expensive way to sell. And doesn't scale.

Look, AI is useful. It's fast. It organizes ideas. It surfaces angles you missed at 2am. I use it every day. That's not the issue.

The issue is what it cannot fake.

A real point of view. Specific proof. Scars from doing the work. The ability to name an objection your buyer hasn't admitted out loud yet (not even to herself).

Buyers are researchers. They read 6-12 of your posts before they ever fill out a form. They're not looking for "value." They're looking for someone who clearly understands them better than they understand themselves.

When you hit that note enough times, the sales call stops being a sales call.

You're not pitching anymore. You're not "qualifying."

You're talking to someone who already decided you were the answer somewhere around post number 7.

Curious where you land on this: are you using AI to write your posts, or to think through them? Different answers, different outcomes.

Ask a senior SQL Server DBA what they think of non-native database backups and you'll get one word: no.

It's not stubbornness. It's scar tissue.

A generation of "SQL-aware" backup tools that truncated the log outside of a real backup. VM snapshots taken without VSS coordination that looked fine until a restore revealed inconsistent data and log files. Backup jobs reporting success while silently breaking the LSN chain. DR tests that failed because nobody actually understood what a recoverable backup required.

The log chain is what defines recoverability — not job status, not file size, not what shows up in your backup software's dashboard. Senior DBAs know this because they've watched strategies that looked solid fall apart when it actually mattered.

The thing is, that instinct — while earned — can also leave you stuck. Because when your database is 8TB and your backup window doesn't exist, "just use native backups" stops being an answer.
 
VSS-based snapshots done right — with the SQL Writer actually participating, the LSN anchor captured, and log backups running independently — can be a legitimate part of a recovery strategy. Done wrong, they're just a faster way to end up with something you can't restore from.

The difference is understanding what's actually happening at the engine level.

What convinced you （or didn't） to trust a 3rd Party SQL Server backup approach?

🛑 STOP giving your business AI agents more power and access than you would ever give a human! 🛑

AI is incredible. I'm no Luddite! I use it every day and its market applicability continues to grow. However, autonomous business agents are not a silver bullet and they should never be given the keys to anything they are capable of single-handedly destroying (or shouldn't have access to for legal/compliance reasons).

I'm not saying don't use autonomous agents. I'm not saying don't use OpenClaw-powered browser automations or Claude Code. They're great tools. What I'm saying is you need to keep the blast radius around them contained, just like you would with a human contributor.

We often put small, intentional barriers in work between humans (or even between steps of a single human's work flow) - for example, the assignment of temporary system permissions. So, why do we do this? Lots of reasons. They could make a mistake. They could fundamentally misunderstand their task. They could get a computer virus. All sorts of things can go wrong!

The same idea applies to your agent, no matter how well-designed. It can make mistakes, and then it can double down on those mistakes. It can get hit with a prompt injection attack from something you or it downloaded. Or it can make any number of other unforced errors we all know it's capable of making.

Now, again, none of these are reasons not to use the tools.

Let me repeat: NOTHING I have said should lead you to believe these tools are useless. They aren't. In many cases, they provide power and utility that was unfathomable a few short years ago.

What I AM saying is that these agents are not better or smarter than humans. They just, for the most part, have a much better "memory" and processing speed than us.

Let me repeat that, too: modern AI agents are not better at reasoning or critical thinking than skilled humans.

So, what's the practical upshot here? It's pretty simple: treat your agents more like people. And no, I don't mean give them health benefits and ask about their kids. I mean you need to take the time to develop an accurate estimation of their capabilities and trustworthiness, then make honest judgment calls about how much risk your business can afford to absorb.

Want to let that OpenClaw agent pilot your browser for the next week so it can perform some focused tasks for you? Awesome! Just make sure it's piloting a browser that only has access to the things you want it to have access to.

Want to use Claude Code (or a custom agent) for agentic programming? Great! You just need to constrain its permissions so it can't blow away your database or force-rebase over your old git commits.

There are edge cases here, like certain types of solopreneur, but they rarely apply to revenue-drawing business systems. And, typically, those people WOULD just hand those keys over to a human, because they have no choice.

You should be embracing agentic AI...just do it responsibly!

Donors don't stop giving because they stop caring.

They stop giving because giving stopped feeling necessary.

It's rarely a dramatic breakup (although those are the ones we see and over-index on). Usually, things just get tight, personally, or the world just feels uncertain, and small prioritization decisions start to happen in the background. The subscriptions. The memberships. The charitable gifts. The ones that feel optional get pushed to later. Later becomes next year. Next year becomes never. 

And….you’ve lost the donor.

What determines whether your org makes that cut is how connected that donor feels to what you're actually doing right now.

A donor who feels like a partner thinks – this org is doing important work and they rely on my gifts. I can't let them down. Sure, maybe the donor gives a little less than last year. But they give. And that matters more than you think.

A donor who feels like a transaction thinks – I'll give next year when things settle down.

Both donors cared about your mission when they first gave. The difference between them isn't passion. It's whether you made them feel like their gift mattered. Specifically, personally, right now.

In a moment when donors are slower to give, foundational stewardship isn't a nice-to-have. It's what determines who stays and who becomes a maybe next year.
hook: Donors don't stop giving because they stop caring.

Most executive coaching engagements can't answer one question:
"What changed?"

Not "how did it feel." Not "what did you learn." What changed — in behaviour, in the people around them, in the business.
If the only evidence is the leader's own reflection six months later, you don't have a coaching outcome. You have an expensive friendship.

Here's the uncomfortable truth: the coaching industry has trained buyers to accept testimonials as proof. "Transformational." "Life-changing." "I see things differently now." Lovely. Unmeasurable.
Meanwhile every other line item on the L&D budget is being asked to show ROI, lift, or behavioural change against a baseline. Coaching gets a pass because we've all agreed not to look too closely.
That pass is closing.

CFOs are asking. Boards are asking. The next generation of HRDs — raised on dashboards — are asking.

The coaches who'll still be billing premium rates in three years are the ones who:
→ Baseline behaviour at the start (self + 180°/360° perception) → Re-measure the same behaviours mid- and post-engagement → Report divergence — what the leader thinks vs. what their people see → Tie shifts to outcomes the business already tracks

You don't need to become a data scientist. You need to stop being afraid of evidence.
Measurement isn't the enemy of the coaching relationship. It's what makes the relationship defensible.
Full piece in comments. 👇

Here's a take you probably won't hear from the pure-cloud vendors: hybrid deployment isn't a transitional state that enterprises tolerate on their way to full cloud migration. For a significant portion of the market, think healthcare, government, financial services, and any organization running mission-critical infrastructure, etc., hybrid is the correct strategic destination. And the vendors who can't or won't acknowledge that are leaving real enterprise requirements on the table.

That was one of the most important things
Mitel
CTO
Luiz Domingos
said in our recent conversation on the Experience Matters podcast, and it's a view I share. The pandemic-era assumption that cloud equals resilience has been stress-tested. Cloud solutions fail. And for organizations where uptime isn't a preference but a regulatory and operational requirement, the risk calculus is fundamentally different.

We covered a lot of ground in this conversation. Mitel's two major product launches — Mitel Edge (infrastructure modernization without forced cloud migration) and Mitel WX (a workforce experience platform built specifically for frontline workers) — are responding to real gaps in what the enterprise communications market has delivered. The AI discussion was equally grounded: Luiz made the case for language model agnosticism, edge AI deployment, and human augmentation over human replacement — all of which are positions I'd put in the "saying the quiet part out loud" category for this industry.

A few things that stood out to me specifically:
The frontline workforce has been underserved by UC platforms built primarily for knowledge workers, and the business case for closing that gap is enormous.
AI in communications is moving from pilot to operational, and the fastest ROI is in contact center — intelligent routing, real-time assist, and automated resolution workflows.

Agentic AI will move enterprise communications from "systems of assistance" to "systems of action,” where workflows execute based on events, not on someone clicking a button.

Voice is having a renaissance as the primary human-AI interface, particularly for frontline use cases.

European enterprises are increasingly demanding fully sovereign communications infrastructure, a trend with significant implications for global vendors.

Our highest-impact people have stopped fitting their job titles.
 
The best "PM" on a recent project wrote more production code than most of our engineers. The best "Engineer" spent half his time in customer calls, reframing the problem. The person who built our most useful internal tool holds no engineering title at all.
 
This isn't an accident. In the recent past, I kept seeing the same thing: when AI handles execution, value moves to judgment, systems thinking, and the ability to turn a messy problem into something that works at scale. Titles capture none of that.
 
So I've started thinking in five dimensions of value captured in five job profiles than titles: builders, reviewers, navigators, operators, specialists.
 
This raises a harder question. If titles no longer predict impact, what shape should an organization actually take?
 
I think that's the most strategic problem of the AI era. And the popular take, that AI makes HR and org design less important, has it exactly backwards.
 
Full piece below

⭐️Wondering the connection between Impressionism and AI?⭐️

In 1839 the camera arrived in Paris. Within twenty years, it had emptied out the function painters had been paid for since the Renaissance.

Some migrated. They stopped depicting reality and started depicting perception. We call them the Impressionists, and we tell their story as a victory.
AI is doing the same thing to knowledge workers now, so we reach for that story to comfort ourselves. Humans always find higher ground.

But Impressionism is the story of the few who survived. For every Monet there was a Sarah Goodridge — a Boston portrait miniaturist who supported her family with her brush until photography quietly emptied her profession. We don't remember her name. History only records the survivors.

By 1870 every middle-class person in Europe instinctively knew how to pose for a camera. Chin up. Shoulders relaxed. Gaze off-axis. Nobody had been taught. The technology had quietly rewritten how an entire civilization stood in front of one another. They thought it was just how a person stood.

We are posing for AI now. Not with our bodies, with our cognition. We ask ChatGPT first. We write in structures the algorithm reads well. We optimize ourselves for AI before we even know we are doing it.

AI will keep arriving. Moving with it is not the question. The question is the pose. And the pose is yours.

I haven't posted much recently because I've gone pretty deep down the rabbit hole into building again.

Over the last 20 years, I've had the chance to build companies, invest in founders, support startups, and spend time around hundreds of businesses across multiple technology cycles.

What's pulled me back in this time is a very different way of looking at work. More specifically, a very different way of looking at coordination.

For a lot of businesses, the work increasingly is coordination.

Not task completion. Coordination. Between people, between teams, between businesses, between constantly changing information, timelines, dependencies, conversations, and decisions.

And over time, context itself becomes the bottleneck.

That realization changed how I started thinking about AI. Not as something that replaces people. As something that can help people work together better.
That idea sent me deep.

For months I've been spending time with contractors, tradespeople, operators, event managers, and homeowners. Visiting job sites. Buying coffee. Watching how the work actually happens.

One thing became clear very quickly: The real work often doesn't live inside software. 

It lives in conversations, voice notes, texts, emails, photos, documents, relationships, and memory. The people holding all of that together are carrying enormous amounts of operational context in their heads, and every tool ever built has asked them to stop what they're doing and feed it data first.

That's what led us to build

38 years in QA. 16 industries. I've watched a lot of things go wrong.

AI adoption is going wrong in the same way.

Not because businesses are picking bad tools. Because they're skipping the conversation that should happen before any tool gets near a real process.

I've sat in rooms where a vendor has just left and nobody can answer basic questions. What exactly are we changing? Who owns it if something breaks? How will we know if it's actually working — or just busy?

Nobody thinks those are controversial questions. But they don't get asked until something breaks.

So I put together a plain-language plan. Five stages. Fifty questions. The ones I'd ask before I'd sign off on anything.

Stage one is just: do you actually know what you're trying to fix? Not in general. Specifically. Which process. Which team. What it costs when it goes wrong today.

Most businesses can't answer that cleanly. That's not a criticism — it's the work.

Stage two is data. Can you legally use the data you're planning to feed into this thing? Who checked? When? These aren't compliance box-ticks — they're the questions that come back to bite you six months in.

Stage three is risk. Not 'AI is risky' in the abstract. Concrete stuff. What happens if it produces wrong output? Who catches it? Is there actually a human in the loop or has that become a formality?

Stage four is the pilot. Run it small. Define what success looks like before you start — not after. And define what failure looks like. If you can't name the thing that would make you stop, you won't stop.

Stage five is the decision. Scale, iterate, pause, or stop. The organisations that get this right aren't the ones who scale fastest. They're the ones willing to say 'not yet' when the evidence doesn't support it.

At the end of all fifty questions there's a scoring guide. But I'll be honest — the score matters less than the gaps it surfaces. If your team can't agree on three of these questions, that's where the real risk sits.

I've made **the whole thing free. No form. No follow-up sequence.**

If you're mid-adoption and something feels off — send me the three questions your team couldn't answer confidently. That's usually where the conversation worth having starts.

Download the plan for yourself (the link is in the comments).

Three years ago,
Pauline Dissake
walked up to me while I was holding a trash bag.

(not exactly the opening scene I would have chosen, but here we are)

I was helping Facilities clean up after a long, hard onsite event day. Nothing catastrophic had happened, but a few small “lessons learned” were replaying in my head, and one particularly impassioned man had just given me 12 minutes of “feedback” about how disappointed he was that there weren’t enough outlets near his chair and that the coffee lids were “not intuitive.”

—Outwardly, I was giving my best performance of concern & openness to feedback… but I spent most of those 12 minutes calculating whether I could still afford daycare if I switched to a career selling chicken tenders on a beach somewhere—

I digress. 

Planning events is funny that way, though. You can spend months building the strategy, designing the experience, anticipating every contingency, and quietly solving a hundred problems no one will ever know existed.

BUT if the room is three degrees too cold, the microphone cuts out for ten seconds, or if two entrée options — selected after accommodating 23 allergies, 11 preferences, and one very unforgiving venue contract — somehow still “lacked flavor”… suddenly those few, small moments that went wrong overshadow the hundreds of big things that went exactly right.. 

So, needless to say, by that point, I was exhausted and just 𝙙𝙤𝙣𝙚.

Then I heard a quiet voice behind me.
“Excuse me, are you Camille?”

…ｄｅｐｅｎｄｓ…

At the time, I had no idea who the woman standing before me was.

I didn’t know what she did.

I honestly don’t even remember exactly what she said… but I will never forget how she changed the way I 𝙛𝙚𝙡𝙩 in that moment.

She went out of her way to tell me how great she thought the event was and how much she appreciated the small details I didn’t think anyone had even noticed.

To her, it may have been a thoughtless, passing gesture…but to me, it was just what I needed.

—

This encounter really stuck with me— not because of 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 Pauline said, but because she stopped to say it in the first place. 

It made me think about how often I think something nice but keep it to myself; because I feel awkward, or the timing feels off...
or because  I assume they ‘probably already know’….

But since the car ride home, that day I met Pauline, I set a challenge for myself: 𝙉𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙧 𝙡𝙚𝙖𝙫𝙚 𝙖 𝙠𝙞𝙣𝙙 𝙩𝙝𝙤𝙪𝙜𝙝𝙩 𝙪𝙣𝙨𝙥𝙤𝙠𝙚𝙣 … because it has such power to shift someone’s whole day.

Now…
Wait for it.

As of this month— and by some twist of fate and universal alignment— Pauline and I work on the same team in Life Science Communications, building employee campaigns, programming and experiences that help people feel more connected, included, and seen.

A full-circle moment. 

So, cheers to my friend Pauline, to lifting others up, seeing the work behind the work, and finding the people who make the hard days feel a little lighter.
#itswhatwedo

Most AI agents never survive the security review. Or the compliance review. Or the infrastructure review.

A team builds something compelling with an AI tool. They take it to the team who is responsible for the production environment, then the questions start:

Who's using this? What data is being sent in? Where is that data? Where does it run? Can you replay what happened? Does the output drift over time? Where's the audit trail? What changed between this version and the last one? 

The tool they used to build the agent can't answer any of these questions.

That's the real reason AI isn't spreading through organisations. Because governance, compliance, and security are asking entirely reasonable questions that the current generation of AI tooling was never built to answer.

You see the output. But the input? The tooling trace? The full run log? It’s locked away, or it doesn't exist at all.

Leadership can't approve what they can't see inside. And they shouldn't.

Since we announced our raise last week, we've spoken to dozens of businesses trying to roll out AI agents. Every conversation hits this same wall.

This is the gap we built Rightbrain to close. Every agent run is logged. Every input and output is traceable. Every model decision is replayable. Every update to an agent is versioned. Change management controls are a default. Agents run on enterprise cloud infrastructure. Governance gets visibility without slowing down the teams that are building.

The gap between AI agent demo and AI agent in production isn't a strategy problem. It's an infrastructure one.

If this is a conversation you're having internally, happy to share how we're solving it. DMs open.
hook: Most AI agents never survive the security review. Or the compliance review. Or the infrastructure review.

Everyone is learning how to build a catalog item with AI. 

I think we're asking the wrong question.

AI is going to change the ServiceNow service ecosystem forever. Same as it is changing every other tech services ecosystem. That part isn't controversial.

And honestly, the work I'm seeing is impressive. Initiatives, projects, products. 

YouTube has many videos showing you how to build a catalog item with AI in minutes. The craft on display is real.

But I can't shake one thought.

Are we not just replaying the digital transformation era?

Back then, plenty of companies "adopted" the shift by swapping legacy tools for SaaS and Cloud. New tools, same processes. Same business model. Same operating model. They changed what they bought, not how they worked.

And we all saw the gap that opened up. Legacy organisations running modern software on top of unchanged ways of working. 

And next to them, the digital natives who built around the technology from day one and invented entirely new business models.

The tool was never the point. The rethink was.

So here's what I keep coming back to. Instead of using AI to build the catalog item faster, shouldn't we be using AI to ask whether the catalog item needs to exist at all?

Faster is not the same as fundamental.

Curious where others land on this. Are you seeing teams use AI to rethink the work, or mostly to speed up the work they already had?
hook: Everyone is learning how to build a catalog item with AI.

AI coding agents are moving faster than the controls around them.

The weak point is not “can the model write code?”

The weak points are:
   ---=[ Who approved the action? ]=---
   ---=[ What did it read? ]=---
   ---=[ What did it execute? ]=---
   ---=[ What state changed? ]=---
   ---=[ Can you replay the session? ]=---
   ---=[ Can you prove the log was not tampered with? ]=---
   ---=[ What happens when the safety sidecar fails? ]=---

I’m building * Skuld * around a simple rule: autonomous agents should be treated like untrusted operators until proven otherwise.

That means typed state, audit trails, operator approval, fail-closed gates, and replayable execution history.

I’m looking for security/platform teams already experimenting with Claude Code, Gemini, Codex, or internal agent swarms. I want to compare notes.

🔐 Picture this scenario: Your team rolled out MFA. You are still getting phished (yes - it can and does happen).

Adversary-in-the-middle kits don't crack passwords. They sit between the user and the real sign-in page, proxy the login, and steal the session token. 

The push gets approved. The attacker still gets in.

That's the gap most "Zero Trust" projects never close.

In a world full of easy fake I'll guarantee you that authenticity wins. 

I sat down at the profile photo 📸  booth at the
JPMorganChase
event in Detroit last week for my free headshots. The system took my photos and then immediately offered some 💇♂️ touch ups. I declined. Moments later I received a link to download my photos with an advanced touch up menu. I declined. When I opened my photos on the
Apple
I was warn down enough with offers to address imprefections that I clicked the touchup 🪄 button. Then undo.

Every time I write a post I get prompts from Grammerly,
Google
Gemini, and
LinkedIn
itself to 'improve' my posts. I have tried each of them and vacillated between second guessing myself and posting original content. I can say I pick original every time 💯. I would further bet anyone a crisp hundo 💵 that I can tell every time AI has been used on a post or email, photo or text, if I've met them in person previously. Try me. 

So lets say we haven't yet met. And you've posted an AI photo, negotiated our meetup with AI language, and enhanced your profile with AI strong enough to transition your college 'barista gig' to 'provisioner of premium agricultural substances on behalf of a multinational.' Now what? It's all BS and you are too. I'll ask a few questions, if we get that far, and you're done. Time well wasted. 

We're finding our amazing clients by keeping it real. Not artificially real like your boy Clavicular, but authentically real like the Millionaire Next Door (must read). Imperfections in the photos, occasional type-o's from excitedly clicking a share of good news, and phone calls ☎️ over text and email.  

So if you're struggling to win in this fray of fake, try real. Post the messy photo with the zit, write how you feel, and talk to strangers. I promise you you'll stand out.

body:
When things go wrong, most leaders become loud and conspicuous.

They talk more. They command. They try to know all the answers.

But leadership is not about who has the loudest voice. It’s about who keeps their head when things fall apart.

The truth is the greatest leaders are the often the ones who say the least.

Here’s 10 quiet ways to be a master in a crisis.

1️⃣ Re-group the troops
↳ People need direction. Anchor them with decisive actions. 

2️⃣ Speak up to halt rumours 
↳ Step in quickly. Clear facts maintain trust and stop second-guessing.

3️⃣ Admit to what you don’t know
↳ Pretending only causes alarm. Share what is known and unknown.

4️⃣ Absorb the pressure
↳ Reassure your team. Offer them a credible recovery plan.

5️⃣ Be visible and available
↳ A stable leader reduces panic. Actively listen and provide calm, confident leadership.

6️⃣ Be decisive, yet flexible
↳ Act on the information you have. Be willing to adapt if things change.

7️⃣Establish the priorities
↳ Priortise critical issues, such as team wellbeing. Provide support.

8️⃣ Stay human when uncertainty mounts
↳ Show you care. Communicate with transparency and empathy. 

9️⃣ Demonstrate belief when morale drops
↳ Be a rock in the storm. Share a clear, reassuring roadmap ahead.

🔟 Be grounded
↳ Provide an alternative to panic. Empower your team to make decisions.

Leaders don’t need to be loud. They need to be the anchor. ⚓

When a storm hits, people don’t need a leader with a big ego:

👉🏻 They need one who won’t bring chaos. 

👉🏻 They need one who quietly reassures and brings stability. 

👉🏻 They need one who makes them feel safe enough to keep going.

People don’t need noise in a crisis. They need a beacon of trust.

And that beacon becomes the leader that everyone follows, through the tough times as well as the good. 👣

Three weeks ago I stood in front of a Miró painting in Barcelona, and I have not stopped thinking about it since - for reasons that have very little to do with art.

We are not facing an AI productivity revolution.

We are facing a curiosity recession.

And most leaders haven't noticed, because the outputs still look fine.

At work, I see team members hand the model the question and bring back the answer. The hypothesis-forming step disappears. The "I sat with this for two days and changed my mind" step disappears. What is left is the output. And the output is usually pretty good.

That is the trap.

Because a team that produces good answers is not the same as a team that can produce good thinking. The difference does not show up immediately. It shows up the first time the model is confidently wrong, and the person holding the answer has no developed instinct for noticing.

I see the same pattern at home with my daughter. The aha moment - that slow, private thrill of figuring something out yourself - is being quietly commoditized.

The reframe I have started using, in both worlds: 

AI is a knowledge amplifier. We are the sensors.

The leaders who get this right will not be the ones who use AI to replace human thinking. They will be the ones who use it to protect the conditions under which real thinking, and real human presence, can still happen.
Full article below. Are you leading a team of producers of cognition, or consumers of it?

Genuinely curious what you are seeing.
#AI
#leadership
#progress
#curiosity
#learning

body:
THE bully in the little things at work ... MICRO- BULLYING 

Microbullying is perhaps best described as bullying by a thousand small cuts.

It’s the small cuts that leave a deep mark: being ignored in the break room, talked over in a meeting, met with an eye roll or wounded by a “just joking” remark that feels anything but funny.

This is what is increasingly being labelled as “microbullying”.

Harder to detect that more overt workplace mistreatment, microbullying is made up of repeated slights, snubs and put-downs.

At first glance, these actions might seem minor in isolation.  

Over time, however, they can wear away confidence, belonging and wellbeing.

It covers behaviours that might slip into that murky space between outright rudeness and obvious bullying. 

Such behaviours are not always dramatic enough to trigger formal complaints.

And they are often too subtle to be addressed adequately by a workplace policy. 

That said, these actions can still be powerful enough to make someone dread coming to work, second-guess their contribution or retreat from the very conversations where their contribution is needed most.

In many workplaces, microbullying shows up as subtle exclusion. 

A person is not copied into emails that matter. The same person might be overlooked when opportunities arise. 

And they find out about changes after everyone else seems to know. 

Each incident might have a reasonable-sounding explanation. Yet the pattern of behaviour sends a clear message: this person does not fully belong.

Microbullying can also appear through small acts of undermining. 

A colleague’s idea is ignored until someone else repeats it or their contribution is met with a smirk. 

A mistake is mentioned repeatedly, long after it has been fixed. 

Questions are asked in a tone that suggests incompetence rather than curiosity and feedback is delivered not to help but to humiliate.

Sometimes microbullying is demonstrated through so-called humour. 

The problem with “just joking” is that it often turns poor behaviour into something that is meant to be accepted. 

The person on the receiving end is expected to laugh along, even when the joke is made at their expense.

Workplaces are particularly fertile ground for microbullying because people are required to keep turning up. 

In ordinary life, it is possible to avoid someone who constantly chips away at confidence. 

At work, avoidance is not always an option. 

The person making the small cuts might be a manager, a team member, a senior colleague or someone with social influence. 

That can mean that the target may feel they have little choice but to endure it.

Repeated small behaviours that make someone feel belittled, excluded or unsafe should not be excused simply because each incident looks minor in isolation.

For twenty years ecommerce only got good at the end of the funnel. 

The checkout. The retarget. The moment you'd already decided.

We built WNTD to own the moment before that. The decision itself.

WNTD makes everything shoppable. Anything you see, anywhere: any retailer, any social feed, any image. Save it, try it on, build a full outfit from six items across completely different stores, and actually see yourself wearing it.
Step into Magic Mirror and see it on you in real time. Real style insight from our AI stylist, not generic waffle. A second opinion from the community. Then it finds how to complete the look, surfaces cheaper alternatives, and the items you didn't know you needed. All of it also inline in our Safari extension while you're already shopping.

No switching tabs. No guessing. No regret.

Here's the part that matters: when people can visualise owning something, they buy it. One month into beta, conversion is already running 3x our previous app and 5-6x the affiliate benchmark. 

Visualisation isn't a feature. It's a conversion engine.

And every save, every try-on, every price watch is an intent signal. Retailers know what you bought. We know what you wanted, often before you did. That dataset compounds with every user, and the incumbents can't build it without breaking their own retailer relationships. That's the moat.

This is the intent layer for agentic commerce. The personalisation everyone's promised for a decade only works when something owns the start of the funnel. 

We do.

Our competitors built one feature each and called it a product. They're cooked.

Built by the team behind Basket: #4 in the UK App Store, £10M GMV, 350k users. Now building the beginning of the funnel, properly.

I’ll be honest: I don’t know exactly what my job will look like in three years. If the pace of change feels uncertain to you, you aren’t alone. Whether you’re just starting out or you’re a veteran leader, we’re all navigating this shift together. While the future is unwritten, one thing is clear: I’m not sitting back to wait and see, and you shouldn’t either.
 
To stay ahead in 2026, we must lean into one fundamental anchor: We don’t hire engineers to write code, we hire them to know what code to write.
 
In a world where the "how" is increasingly automated, your value lies in your judgment and your curiosity. Here’s how to navigate this evolution:

•	Master the "Why": Don’t just execute a ticket; understand the business value. Why does this feature matter to our customers? When you understand the why, you become a strategic partner, not just a resource.
•	Invest in Human Skills: As technical execution gets faster, your ability to present an idea, influence a stakeholder, and lead a team becomes your greatest competitive advantage. Executive presence is now a core engineering skill.
•	Stay Radically Curious: Don’t wait for a training. Dive into new tools, break things, and lead the change. To know what to build, you have to stay grounded in the basics while being the first to embrace the new.
 
We can no longer afford to passively react to change; we have to proactively embrace and drive it. Everyone has access to the same tools we do. Our edge comes from your context, your problem-solving, and your drive. The uncertainty isn't a signal to slow down. It’s a call to be bold, re-skill, and retool. Let’s stop second-guessing what the future looks like and start defining it together.
#SoftwareEngineering
#CareerGrowth Let's Take a Walk: An Open Letter to Software Engineers

Let's say you rent a property out on Airbnb. It's going well, and you'd like to add a second unit, but you need a loan. The best-positioned party to underwrite it is Airbnb itself. 

Here is why: 

Airbnb's payment processor isn't well-positioned to approve this loan. They can see your payment history, but not much beyond that.

The local community bank may do better! However, the underwriter may have to make guesses about unfamiliar areas. And you'd have to commit to the application process itself.

Meanwhile, Airbnb sees your reviews, cancellations, calendar; your property's location, amenities, and comparables; how often travelers search for terms it matches; how long travelers linger over photos of the picture windows.

This is why we think industry-specific platforms, whether they're marketplaces or vertical SaaS, are so well-positioned to make embedded finance plays.
