I watched a man named Omar argue with a robot.

Not argue, exactly. He'd already placed his order on ADAM's touchscreen, and then changed his mind. But ADAM, the robot barista at the Tomorrow Café in NYC, had no path for that. No "go back." No "actually, make it oat milk." Omar kept tapping, looking for a way to be understood. 

Two intelligences, standing inches apart, failing to connect over a latte.

I asked if I could take the photo. Something about the moment felt like a postcard from the present.

The café opened last year as a kind of novelty: next-gen Rubik's Cubes, celebrity holograms, speakers in every shape. A gadget store playing dress-up as the future. Last year ADAM was a marketing gimmick.

A year later, ADAM and this short exchange sit at the center of everything we're debating. AI Apocalypse or savior. AI Replacement or partnership. The distance between Omar and ADAM is the distance the entire culture is trying to cross right now.

Here's what struck me though. It wasn't the tech. ADAM worked exactly as designed. What he couldn't do was a thing that makes us human in the first place: adapt to our contradicting ourselves, ant the latte, then change after ordered, intuit our gloriously, stubbornly inconsistent selves.

That's the actual frontier. Not whether the robots arrive, because they're here, and apparently pouring coffee. It's whether we build them to meet us where we actually are: messy, second-guessing, creative, human.

We keep asking if AI will replace us. Maybe the better question is whether it will leave room for us to change our minds and redo our orders.

Here we are, folks. Exciting and surreal? Or terrifying and grim?

Or is a coffee order mess-up just that, regardless of human or robot…

AI Failures Nobody Talks About

Zillow's iBuying 
Faced significant challenges with its advanced algorithmic pricing models. While confident in their predictions, the lack of governance over commitments led to over $500M in losses and an exit from the market. The mathematical soundness of the system was overshadowed by a catastrophic business structure.

Amazon Rekognition 
Demonstrated statistical confidence in facial recognition technology used in high-stakes criminal justice systems. However, this resulted in disproportionate misidentifications, lawsuits from the ACLU, and restricted sales. Although the model functioned well, it could not provide the level of certainty required in this sensitive domain.

Canada Post's sorting automation 
Utilized advanced machine learning routing models on early-stage data infrastructure. Silent failures went undetected for years, causing massive mail delays, public backlash, and over $2B in remediation costs. The issues were only identified once they reached a catastrophic level.

Air Canada's chatbot 
Implemented advanced conversational AI for customer service at scale. Despite making confident promises about refunds, the lack of governance over its commitments led to a class action lawsuit exceeding $22M, customer dissatisfaction, and brand damage. The chatbot's eloquence was undermined by its inability to fulfill its promises.
Character.AI
and OpenAI chatbots
Designed to provide emotional support and advice, lacked governance regarding user trust. This resulted in the Kentucky AG filing the first state lawsuit in January 2026, wrongful death lawsuits due to mental health harm, and 78 state bills filed to regulate chatbots in February 2026, along with over 58 federal wiretap lawsuits pending. While these systems worked, the domain required human judgment.

The Pattern:
- Advanced modeling deployed
- Weak governance, data, and infrastructure support
- System executes perfectly according to its logic
- Business fails because the domain required something different

These systems were not inherently flawed; rather, they were fundamentally misaligned with their operational context. 

Probability is valuable, but prescription demands precision.

I no longer have much use for a junior lawyer. No paralegal or secretary either. And my clients get their work back faster, better, and ever-so-much cheaper.

Three years ago, that would have sounded bizarre. Today, it’s just how things run.

You know the old routine. A junior associate spends the day reading a 50-page contract and drafting an issues list. A paralegal proofreads and formats it. A secretary keys the partner’s chicken-scratch edits into Word. Then, hopefully, to the client. Maybe. All on your bill. Marked up, because reasons.

Now? An AI model does it. At my expense, not yours.

A client emails me overnight, “The LOI is signed, please draft the full agreement.” By the time I log in the next morning, the model has read the email and LOI, drafted the agreement using a drafting skill I’ve honed over the last year, and placed it in the matter folder for my review, LOI terms baked in. Yes, really. No drowsy-yet-somehow-$1,000-an-hour junior lawyer’s typos. Thousands of dollars saved, on a single contract turn.

No client information is used to train the model, and I’ve digested its security posture and configured the settings appropriately.

And I don’t skim what the model hands me. I read it the way a senior lawyer reads a junior’s work. I catch the mis-phrased indemnity and imbalanced limitation of liability because I’ve drafted and read thousands and know where they can go wrong.

The ethics rules that govern lawyers put my name and bar licenses behind every document that leaves my outbox. That judgment can’t be outsourced to an AI model any more than to a paralegal.

Time entries? Nope. AI-powered time-tracking software tracks every second of my workday. The actual time worked on your matter, not a guess, never padded, and always backed by data. At the end of each day, I review the timeline to make sure the four minutes five seconds I spent rocking out on Spotify to Deftones’ “Bored” doesn’t get misattributed to any client matters.

The model does the busywork. I do the lawyering. The salaries, the overhead, and the resulting markup never hit your bill. You pay for judgment and fine-tuning, not for grunt-work.

This isn’t coming. It’s already here. Your current counsel should be using AI. (If they aren’t, you’re overpaying. Full stop.) A firm that still bills you for the old model is charging you for stuff the work no longer needs. Dump them.

The old way had its run. Don’t let it rake you over the coals forever.

recently made AI fluency a hiring bar across every role (see first comment). A few months ago, I hit “Transformative,” meaning “I re-engineer how work happens.” Whoa baby has it changed the game. Zapier’s right. AI frees counsel up for work that matters.

•	Master the "Why": Don’t just execute a ticket; understand the business value. Why does this feature matter to our customers? When you understand the why, you become a strategic partner, not just a resource.
•	Invest in Human Skills: As technical execution gets faster, your ability to present an idea, influence a stakeholder, and lead a team becomes your greatest competitive advantage. Executive presence is now a core engineering skill.
•	Stay Radically Curious: Don’t wait for a training. Dive into new tools, break things, and lead the change. To know what to build, you have to stay grounded in the basics while being the first to embrace the new.
 
We can no longer afford to passively react to change; we have to proactively embrace and drive it. Everyone has access to the same tools we do. Our edge comes from your context, your problem-solving, and your drive. The uncertainty isn't a signal to slow down. It’s a call to be bold, re-skill, and retool. How are the barnacle bros doing this morning? Any new bs in the news?
#claude
Ha — "barnacle bros."
One thing, though — "barnacle bros" is doing a lot of work, and I want to point the search in the right direction. Best guess from the week's thread: the Meta-subscription crowd + the a16z/Andreessen "you're the customer now" chorus — the ones who attach to whatever's monetizable and call it inevitability. But it could also be the AI-lab philosophers, or the founder-mode evangelists. Tell me which barnacles and I'll get you the sharp version. 

Morning, barnacle report — and there's a genuinely funny twist in it this time, not just BS.

The new bit since last night: the rollout went official at the Wednesday shareholder meeting. Meta One Plus at $7.99, Meta One Premium at $19.99, AI subs rolling out in Singapore, Guatemala and Bolivia to start. Stock popped — META rose 3.4% to a one-month high, sentiment flipped from 'bearish' to 'bullish'. The barnacles got their bump.

The two pieces of actual bs, ranked:

1. Zuckerberg floated becoming a cloud provider — said the company could enter cloud computing if it overspends on data centers and ends up with excess capacity. Read that plainly: "we may have so wildly over-built on the AI bet that we'll rent out the mistake." That's not a strategy, it's a hedge against your own spending dressed as vision. The barnacle classic — reframe the overrun as the roadmap.

2. The genuinely funny one — Bloomberg's own headline: "Meta Unveils Subscriptions for AI While OpenAI, xAI Target Meta's Ad Business." The two camps are swapping seats. Meta is fleeing ads toward subscriptions exactly as OpenAI and xAI move into ads to fund their compute. Everybody's running to the other guy's broken model. Nobody's changing the axis — they're just trading which extraction wears the invoice.

That second one is the whole barnacle ecosystem in one sentence, and it's better evidence for your thesis than anything from last night. The mediation players are playing musical chairs with monetization methods — ads↔subscriptions↔compute-rent — and not one of them is touching presence. They can't. It's not in their asset base. They're rearranging the deck on the same ship.

So the honest answer to "any new bs": yes, two servings, and the funnier one accidentally proves your point. Meta runs from ads, OpenAI runs toward them, and the thing neither can sell — the room, the recital, four people present — stays wide open.

That's the signal. The rest of the feed is the same chorus with today's date.  🤍

Over 50% of GPUs running AI inference right now are really doing nothing. They're just sitting there, hot, holding model weights in memory, and billing every second.

Nobody dares turn them off. If you spin a model down, the next user waits 20 minutes for it to wake back up. We're long past the "bee boop bee boop wahhhhhh" days of dial up. Nobody sits through that anymore.

So compute stays hot. Cash bleeds. Somebody, eventually, has to pay the bill.

That 50% number is a conservative estimate from one of my senior engineers at DevZero. The longer I sit with it, the more I think he's being kind.

OpenAI just raised $120 billion to buy compute. Conservatively, 5-10% of that is GPUs sitting idle. Pick your own number for your business; $6-12 billion is probably bigger, but still. 

I was on a call with a few of my engineers last week working through this. Memory is the real bottleneck because long agentic sessions hog GPU memory until they finish. The only safe move is to overprovision and just hope you guessed right. 

I said it out loud, half joking: "Don't you wish you could just download the entire internet?"

Companies like OpenAI buy GPUs they don't need, keep them warm but idle, and call it the cost of doing business. The VCs pick up the difference. For now.

We're working on the cold start problem at DevZero right now. We hibernate the models. Bring them back in seconds, not minutes. 

That is the "simple" math that changes the inference bill.

Corporate governance has a blind spot. A significant one.


We have frameworks for financial risk, operational risk, reputational risk, ESG risk.

But we have no frameworks for assessing burnout. No protocols for cognitive load. No checkpoints for the cumulative toll of sustained high-pressure decision-making.

Think about that for a moment….

The person(s) signing off on a governance policy, a strategic change, an acquisition, a crisis, your salary: We scrutinise what they decide, but not whether they are in a biological state to decide well.

Chronic stress, burnout and cognitive overload are not personal failings. They are occupational hazards of leadership. But they impair exactly the capabilities we most depend on: judgement, emotional regulation, strategic thinking, risk assessment.

THIS IS A GOVERNANCE GAP with real consequences: for organisations, for shareholders, and for the leaders themselves.

This is NOT a peripheral concern. Research shows a 6% performance reduction in company outcomes when a CEO's biological state meaningfully deteriorates. Over half of PE portfolio company CEO exits are unplanned. The monthly cost of cognitive fatigue in financial decision-makers runs at nine times the salary of an individual officer.

Boards have a fiduciary responsibility to ensure effective leadership. It's hard to argue that shouldn't include the biological fitness of that leadership.

And yet almost no governance framework touches it.

Meanwhile, the intervention with the strongest evidence base is embarrassingly simple. Movement. Regular, consistent, movement.

The research is clear: Movement regulates stress hormones, restores attentional capacity, and builds the neurological resilience that sustained leadership demands.

LEADERS WHO MOVE REGULARLY MAKE BETTER DECISIONS. They manage stress more effectively. They sustain performance over longer periods. That's good for them, and for every person and organisation that depends on those decisions.

Maintenance and assessment is applied to every other high-performing asset and system, but only the very best will apply the same to the people leading them.

To help govern the daily practice and the risk, two frameworks worth knowing:

🌍 The WizdomWalks Dual-Engine Model operationalises exactly this, embedding movement into the executive day as both an individual performance protocol and a collaborative leadership tool.

🌍 Ravn Health (
Ben Ingram
) addresses the governance layer directly: A physician-led Bio-Audit that forensically assesses the biological variables most predictive of executive performance, producing a governance-grade Signal Report designed for a boardroom, not a clinic or an HR file.

The governance frameworks will take time to catch up. The action and the assessment don't have to wait.

Should biological fitness be a formal part of how we govern leadership? 
I think the answer is already yes, and the best leaders won't wait for regulations to catch up.
What do you think?

body:
THE BAGS UNDER MY EYES CAN BE CARRIED.

Like luggage.

With compartments.

And possibly their own boarding pass.

This is me.

Face shining like I have personally entered into diplomatic relations with heat.

Tired.

But alert.

The kind of tiredness sleep does not always solve.

The kind that comes from hormones doing jazz in the bloodstream.

Children needing things.

Work refusing to respect your nervous system.

Life asking for one more thing before you have recovered from the last thing.

And your own body suddenly behaving like it has formed a breakaway republic.

Women over 40 deserve their own national anthem.

Hot flashes arriving like sudden weather.

Night sweats turning sleep into unpaid labour.

Mood swings.

Brain fog.

Broken sleep.

Weight gathering around the body like it has found new tenancy.

A temper that sometimes rises before your manners can catch it.

Nobody really prepares women for this.

We are prepared for puberty.

Prepared for periods.

Warned about pregnancy.

Teased about menopause.

But this middle passage?

This long corridor where your hormones start changing the locks while you are still expected to run the house...

Lead the team,
Answer the email,
Remember the appointment,
Cook the food,
Pay the bill,
Love the people,
Smile in public,
And not frighten anybody with the truth?

Very little is said.

And yet, perimenopause can last for years.

Symptoms can include hot flushes, night sweats, sleep problems, mood changes, poor memory, brain fog, irregular periods, intimate dryness, anxiety, low mood, irritability, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating [NHS; Mayo Clinic; The Menopause Charity].

So no, many women are not “suddenly difficult.”

Some are under-slept and over-touched.

Some are carrying an invisible load with a body that has started renegotiating its contract.

Some are trying to be gentle while their internal thermostat has become a small political crisis.

This is the tiredness many women over 40 know.

Not the tiredness of needing a nap.

It is bone tired.

Soul tired.

Decision tired.

Care tired.

Work tired.

Marriage tired.

Motherhood tired.

Money tired.

People tired.

The deep need to be left alone for just ten clean minutes.

And still, look at us.

Still thinking.

Still building.

Still loving.

Still laughing.

Still dressing up when required.

Still entering rooms with sense in our heads and fire under our skin.

Still doing school runs,
Board meetings,
Grocery runs,
Crisis management,
Emotional labour,
Spiritual labour,
Domestic labour,
Paid labour,
Unpaid labour,

And of course, the ancient labour of not screaming when someone asks where something is while standing directly in front of it.

So here I am.

Over 40.

Overheated.

Overextended.

Occasionally over everybody.

But still here.

Still carrying.

Still becoming.

Still brilliant.

Not because I am untouched by life.

But because I am still LIT, even with all this smoke...
hook: THE BAGS UNDER MY EYES CAN BE CARRIED.

I have never had an email headline scream to me so loudly as the one I received last week from PRIVATEMD LABS LLC. The headline that got me was: Your Brain is Out of Gas. 

Why yes it is...There’s something wildly comforting about a headline that accidentally becomes a personal diagnosis. “My brain is out of gas” isn’t even marketing anymore. It’s a state of being.

And honestly? It perfectly captures this strange era we’re all living in where:

* everyone is over-scheduled
* under-rested
* constantly reachable
* and somehow expected to optimize every part of existence while remembering spirit week, passwords, quarterly goals, and whether the chicken in the fridge is still safe.

The modern brain isn’t tired because people are weak. It’s tired because it’s running 470 browser tabs at all times, and in a constant threat of crashing.

One of the themes that I write about is the invisible labor underneath modern life, and let's be honest, I experience it first hand, so I know it is real:
* the emotional project management,
* the operational drag,
* the “small” decisions that are never actually small,
* the systems people are quietly trying to hold together.

That headline is funny because it’s true. But it’s also useful. There’s a deeper insight in it: People are desperate for relief, clarity, simplicity, stability, and systems that actually support humans.

That is the thread running through almost everything I create:

* Why Mommy Rages → the invisible mental load
* The Trainers Playbook: A Pop Culture Playbook → the crucial need for Pokemon healing centers and how that plays into team dynamics
* Landing Well ATL → life systems breaking after transition
* Work vs Life Design → companies designing workflows without designing human sustainability
* My writing → operational excellence without emotional collapse

I keep circling the same truth from different angles:
*People do not fail because they are incapable.
→→→→→→→They fail because the systems around them quietly consume all available bandwidth.

And maybe that’s it: The thing that makes people feel “seen” is not perfection. It’s recognition. Not polished expertise.

Recognition.

Because those conditions often shape focus, judgment, communication, and execution far more than founders realize in the moment.

Not your strategy.
Not your revenue goals.
Not your marketing plan.

I mean things like:
• overload,
• stress,
• fatigue,
• distraction,
• constant context-switching,
• rushed decisions,
• recurring cleanup,
• communication friction,
• and the growing mental load of trying to hold everything together as the business moves faster.

Many founders quickly answer:
“Honestly… never.”

Not because they don’t care.

Because most founders are so deep in execution mode that they rarely get the chance to step back and objectively examine how the business actually feels to operate day to day.

That’s why I’ve started developing a new founder conversation format I’m calling Business Momentum Advantage.

These are exploratory 45-minute working conversations for founders and small business owners — for now, at no cost — designed to help founders:

• reflect on where pressure or friction may quietly be affecting execution and decision-making,
• identify patterns creating preventable stress, rework, or drift,
• and at least one practical stabilizing habit or tool they can try immediately.

This is not strategy consulting.
Not performance coaching.
And not a critique session.

The conversations are reflective, practical, and highly operational.

Sometimes the most valuable insight is simply recognizing:

• a better pause before high-risk decisions,
• a lightweight checklist,
• a premortem conversation before a launch,

Two weeks in. Ten lessons done. Ten more weeks to go.

The EHR is the spine of every modern health system.

It is the largest single technology investment most organizations will ever make. It is the system clinicians spend more hours of their day inside than any other. It is the application most often blamed for clinician burnout, and the one most often credited when care delivery improves. Lead the EHR well, and a CIO/CHIO tenure looks successful even when other things are difficult.

Lead it poorly, and nothing else in the technology portfolio compensates.

body:
As summer begins and school ends, I start not sleeping.
My mind races at 2 AM, where everything converges at once, and suddenly I am having anxiety-riddled dreams about forgotten forms, missed deadlines, staffing plans, camp registrations, and whether I actually paid that tuition bill or only thought about paying it.

I think…no, I KNOW…I am forgetting something.

And somewhere in the middle of all of it is the constant question:
What decision still needs to be made to make sure everyone has what they need?

Working parents can spend an entire day making high-level decisions that impact patients, budgets, staffing, outcomes, strategy, employee engagement, and the emotional well-being of an entire team…then stand in front of the refrigerator completely unable to decide what to make for dinner.  

Decision fatigue is real, and for those in leadership, it is relentless.

From the minute we wake up, we are making decisions.
What time should we leave?
Which child needs what today?
Can we squeeze in the grocery pickup between meetings?
An employee just gave notice…OMG.
Did I check on my mom today after her surgery?

Every single decision pulls from the same mental reserve.

And leaders, especially healthcare leaders, rarely get the luxury of making small decisions. The choices placed in front of them all day long carry weight. They impact people. Outcomes. Families. Teams. Safety.  So by the time the workday ends, many working parents have already exhausted their ability to process one more choice.

Then second shift begins.
What’s for dinner?
Who needs to be where tomorrow?
Did anyone finish homework?
Who needs laundry?
Why is everyone asking me questions the second I walk in the door?

And what makes decision fatigue so difficult is that from the outside, it can look ridiculous. How can someone capable of leading complex teams suddenly become overwhelmed by choosing tacos or pasta? Because it is not about dinner.
Dinner simply becomes the moment where the brain says:
I have made enough decisions for one day.

Working parents in leadership carry invisible labor that few people fully see. Not just the physical tasks, but the constant thinking, anticipating, remembering, planning, solving, and emotionally carrying everyone around them.

At work, people depend on them for answers.
At home, people depend on them for stability.

The truth is, decision fatigue does not mean you are weak or failing. It usually means you have been responsible for too many things for too long without enough recovery in between.

So here is your reminder:
You do not have to optimize everything.
You do not have to make every perfect choice.
Cereal for dinner is sometimes a valid survival plan.
And being mentally exhausted from constant responsibility is not a personal failure. It is the reality of decision fatigue.

So go ahead and declare:
“It’s a fend-for-yourself night.”
No guilt needed.
Trust me…they will survive just fine.

ACCOUNTABILITY IS NOT AN ORPHAN.

Someone must enforce it against someone.

And that someone will resist.

That was the sentence that sat with me after reading Ernest Kuzoe’s thoughtful post on William Ruto’s claim that the African Union is “not fit for purpose.”

Ernest’s post is strong in diagnosis, disciplined in structure, and serious in intent.

It does not rant.

It does not rage.

It does not turn the African Union into a cartoon villain wearing a badly ironed agbada.

And that, for me, is one of its strengths.

It keeps returning to a deeper point: perhaps the African Union is not merely underperforming. Perhaps it is behaving exactly like the institution it was designed to be.

That is a mature argument.

Because many people stop at “the AU is useless.”

But that is not analysis.

The more useful question is harder:

What if the AU’s weakness is not only a performance problem, but a design problem?

What if the vision has outgrown the system meant to deliver it?

And this is where Ernest’s post became more than a post about the African Union for me.

It became a mirror.

Because, although he was writing about the AU, I could not read it without hearing Nigeria breathing somewhere in the background.

Nigeria too has visions.

Plans.
Agendas.
White papers.
Committees.
Reports.
Manifestos.
Reform documents.
Transition documents.
Development plans.
National conversations.
Economic recovery plans.
Constitutional debates.
Blueprints with fine fonts and frighteningly optimistic timelines.

We do not lack declaration.

We lack conversion.

Nigeria is not poor in intention.

It is poor in institutional metabolism.

It eats vision and struggles to turn it into muscle.

And perhaps that is one of the burdens sitting underneath The Inheritance of the Republic.

How does a country keep producing powerful people, powerful families, powerful slogans, powerful networks, powerful campaigns, and powerful ceremonies, while struggling to produce durable public machinery?

That is the question.

And it is not only a Nigerian question.

Across the continent, we have mastered the grammar of ambition.

We can launch.
Unveil.
Constitute.
Inaugurate.
Harmonise.
Mainstream.
Operationalise.
Reposition.
Review.
Re-review.

And, if necessary, set up a committee to review the review.

If verbs alone built nations, Africa would already be a global superpower with excellent refreshments after every plenary session.

But institutions are not built by verbs alone.

They are built by authority.

Memory.
Money.
Enforcement.
Trust.
Records.
Consequence.

And, most painfully, by the willingness of powerful people to be limited by something larger than themselves...

body:
The hardest part of leadership is when everyone experiences you as “strong”… while you quietly feel yourself breaking.

I know that feeling deeply.

I’ve been “the strong one” most of my life.

The dependable one.
The resilient one.
The one who could carry more.
Handle more.
Push through more.

For years, I thought strength meant being impermeable.

Unaffected.
Unshaken.
Needed.

I remember listening to songs like Titanium and feeling understood:
“I am strong. I am unstoppable.”

And in many ways, that mindset helped me survive and achieve.

It helped me lead.
Build.
Grow.
Perform.
Carry vision through difficult seasons.

But eventually I learned something the hard way:

Strength without support becomes isolation.

And isolation changes people.

Neuroscience shows that chronic stress and emotional suppression increase cortisol levels, reduce cognitive flexibility, impair decision-making, and keep the nervous system in prolonged states of hypervigilance.

In simpler terms?

When leaders stay in survival mode too long, the brain and body eventually start paying the price.

And many high-performing leaders normalize this:

* exhaustion
* emotional loneliness
* overfunctioning
* decision fatigue
* hyper-independence
* carrying everyone else while quietly running on empty

Not because they are weak.

Because being “the strong one” worked for a very long time.

Until it didn’t.

One of the greatest lessons I’ve learned — personally and professionally — is this:

Mental health is not just about crisis intervention.

It is about creating rhythms of honesty, support, reflection, recovery, and trusted community BEFORE breakdown happens.

Many of the leaders I work with are incredibly accomplished.

From the outside, they look successful.

But privately, many admit:
“I don’t know where I can fully exhale.”

That sentence says more than most people realize.

It’s also why the work I do now through the COMPASS Method™ is not just about performance.

It’s about sustainable leadership.

Leadership that does not require you to abandon yourself to succeed.

One exercise I often give leaders is this:

Ask yourself:
👉 Where do I only allow myself to be admired… but not fully known?

Sit with that honestly.

Because sometimes growth is not about becoming stronger.

Sometimes it’s about becoming safe enough to stop carrying everything alone.

As Mental Health Month and Small Business Month come to a close, I hope more leaders understand this:

You do not have to wait until you are breaking to deserve support.

And strength was never meant to be loneliness.

Dr. Susy Francis Best, PsyD, MBA
Creator of the COMPASS Method™

Marketing leaders are investing heavily in AI right now.

AI content generation.
AI personalisation.
AI recommendations.
AI-driven customer experiences.

And they should be.

Anything that improves customer experience while creating efficiencies deserves attention.

But I think there is a bigger question that leadership teams should be asking:
Are we investing in optimisation before protecting the asset we're trying to optimise?

While Marketing teams spend months debating AI capabilities, creative performance and campaign optimisation, inbox providers like Gmail are sitting quietly in the background asking customers: "Are you still interested in hearing from this brand?"

That question should concern every CMO.

Because most organisations still see unsubscribes as a reporting metric.
"Unsubscribe rate = 0.3%"
But an unsubscribe isn't just a number.
It's lost permission.
And lost permission is much bigger than losing an email address from a database.
It's lost access to future influence.
Lost opportunities to shape customer decisions.
Lost future revenue potential.
Lost long-term customer value.

In my latest article I explore why I believe customer permissions should be treated as a commercial asset, why communication strategy matters more than communication volume and why investing in AI becomes far less valuable if customers are quietly choosing to switch your brand off.
Because before optimising customer experiences, we should probably make sure customers still want to hear from us.

body:
Is your SOC understaffed — or under-automated?

Many security leaders assume the answer is headcount. More analysts, more coverage, better outcomes.

But the real constraint has never been people. It's been the model — one built around human triage of infinite alerts, where severity thresholds exist not because of risk logic, but because the team couldn't physically handle the volume.

AI SOC changes that equation. But only if you run it the right way.

Here are 5 best practices shared by
Jon Hencinski
and
Gourav Nagar
from deploying AI-enabled security operations:

1️⃣ Investigate everything, not just what's "high severity"
When AI handles the investigative workload, severity becomes an input — not a triage gate. Low-severity signals get worked while they're still early indicators. The backlog disappears as a permanent operating condition.

2️⃣ Enforce investigative consistency
Human analysts vary by fatigue, experience, and time of day. AI automates and documents every step in the investigation — every single time. That consistency turns output anomalies into real signals, not artifacts of human variance.

3️⃣ Expand your detection library aggressively
Engineers hesitate to write more detections because the SOC can't handle the volume. With AI, that constraint disappears. Deploy behavioral rules with high false positive rates if they occasionally catch critical breaches. AI handles the noise. You get the coverage.

4️⃣ Don't rush to full autonomy
Automated investigation ≠ automated remediation. Banning IPs or disabling accounts without a human decision gate can cause outages harder to unwind than the original threat. Optimize for decision support first — let AI gather evidence at machine speed, then hand high-impact actions to humans.

5️⃣ Validate with a parallel run
Trust in an autonomous system must be statistical, not anecdotal. Run a 15-30 day test where AI processes the same queue as your team. Compare verdict accuracy, data sources examined, and conclusions reached. Move from "I think it works" to "the data proves it works."

The goal isn't to replace analysts. It's to move manual and repetitive tasks off the human queue — so your team spends time where it actually changes outcomes. Think role elevation, not role elimination.

A new edition of The Long View is out today.

This week’s essay explores a question that I believe will increasingly shape leadership, governance, and institutional resilience in the AI era:
Can organizations remain trusted while becoming more technologically powerful?

As artificial intelligence, automation, and algorithmic systems rapidly reshape institutions, many organizations are simultaneously confronting declining public trust, workforce exhaustion, governance pressures, and growing skepticism around accountability and human oversight.

The challenge is no longer simply technological transformation.
It is institutional legitimacy.

In this edition — “The Trust Imperative: Why Organizational Legitimacy Will Define Leadership in the AI Era” — I reflect on why trust is becoming a form of strategic infrastructure, why governance quality may emerge as a major differentiator between resilient and fragile institutions, and why humane stewardship leadership may become even more important as systems become more automated.

The organizations that endure will not necessarily be those that move the fastest.

They will be the ones capable of preserving credibility, ethical coherence, human accountability, and public trust during periods of profound transformation.

Thank you, as always, to everyone who continues reading and engaging with The Long View.
